speakeroldname: Hon. Sidney E. Smith (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: STATEMENT AS TO REPRESENTATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Ottawa West yesterday directed a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce concerning United States mandatory oil import restrictions, and asked whether the Canadian government had made any representations to the United States government opposing mandatory restrictions or regulations.
My colleague the Minister of Trade and Commerce indicated that the Canadian government's position on this matter had been stated very clearly at the meeting of the Canada-United States joint committee on trade and economic affairs in Ottawa early in January, that its position remained unchanged, and that this had been so indicated to the authorities in Washington. The method used to reiterate the Canadian government's point of view was a note from the Canadian charge d'affaires in Washington to the acting secretary of state delivered on February 19, 1959, a copy of which I am now tabling.
The note made it clear that the Canadian government continues to believe that there is no justification on grounds of security, or for that matter on any other grounds, for United States restrictions on oil imports from Canada, pointing out that such restrictions were incompatible with the need of the two countries to pool their oil resources in time of common emergency. The note further
pointed out that a system of mandatory controls on imports from Canada would be even more disturbing to the Canadian government than a system of voluntary controls, to which the Canadian government had already expressed its opposition.
The purpose of sending the note at that time was to request the United States department of state to bring the Canadian government's views to the attention of those concerned with the review then in progress of United States oil import regulations. We were subsequently informally notified that the action requested was duly taken by the state department.
By leave of the house, Mr. Speaker, I ask that the text of the Canadian note of February 19, 1959 be printed as an appendix to the House of Commons debates of today.

speechtext: Since the note is dated February 19, I wonder if the Secretary of State for External Affairs, in view of the request of the President of the United States that there should be an extension before the final decision on March 10, could say whether or not there are now negotiations under way or about to begin between Canada and her opposite numbers in the United States.

maintopic: URANIUM-STATEMENT ON AGREEMENT WITH JAPAN

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. Sidney E. Smith (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: URANIUM-STATEMENT ON AGREEMENT WITH JAPAN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the Leader of the Opposition addressed a question to me in which he inquired what progress had been made with regard to negotiations with the government of Japan for a bilateral agreement on the peaceful uses of atomic energy. He also inquired, Mr. Speaker, when those negotiations began.
First I would draw the attention of the Leader of the Opposition to the reply I gave on February 26 to question No. 163, which is relevant to the second part of his question.
This is the present situation. Last year we informed the Japanese government of our desire to negotiate an agreement with them with respect to the peaceful uses of atomic energy. During recent months our embassy in Tokyo has carried forward discussions with officials of the Japanese foreign ministry on this subject. The point has now been reached where the way appears to be open for formal negotiations to begin. We have invited the Japanese authorities to send a delegation to Ottawa at their earliest convenience and we are confident that they will soon come to Canada. As I informed the house on February 2, the formal negotiations, we hope, can be concluded in the spring of this year.
There is one other point relevant to this subject which is worth recalling to the attention of hon. members, and that is that last December 12 the government offered three


metric tons of natural uranium to the international atomic energy agency, free of charge, which the agency will supply to Japan this year for use in their atomic energy program. The then acting minister of trade and commerce made an announcement to that effect on December 12. I may add that since then the Canadian offer has been accepted and the final details of the arrangements for transferring the uranium to Japan are now being worked out with the agency in Vienna.
This will be the first step in what we hope will be a long and mutually beneficial association between Canada and Japan in the field of co-operation for the peaceful use of atomic energy.

maintopic: URANIUM-STATEMENT ON AGREEMENT WITH JAPAN

All I can
say is that we have pressed for it, and the Japanese authorities at that time were not as prompt as we expected they would be.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR MOVEMENT OF TOUGH AND DAMP GRAIN

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: PROVISION FOR MOVEMENT OF TOUGH AND DAMP GRAIN
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. In view of the large amount of tough and damp grain still on farms, particularly in the northeastern part of Saskatchewan, can the minister inform the house whether quotas will be raised and priority on box cars will be given to have this grain shipped out before the mild weather sets in, and thus avoid spoilage?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gordon Churchill (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
maintopic: PROVISION FOR MOVEMENT OF TOUGH AND DAMP GRAIN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon.
member for Mackenzie, as well as other hon. members from northern Saskatchewan, drew this matter to my attention the other day. I discussed the situation with the wheat board last fall, and over the intervening months considerable effort has been made to move from that area of Saskatchewan some of the tough and damp grain stored there. The report of the wheat board on the present position is as follows:

The Canadian wheat board has been watching the delivery position in northeastern Saskatchewan very carefully and is taking every action possible to ensure that damp grain in particular may be moved off farms prior to the advent of warm weather.
In this connection quotas are being increased automatically to the full extent of the elevator space available in the area. In an endeavour tc maximize the quotas as early as possible in the areas affected, priority in box car supply has been given for the movement of tough and damp grain. On February 18 last the board issued instructions to the railways to discontinue placing cars on an out-of-order basis to the lakehead except for the movement of tough and damp grain.
The effect of this order is to restrict the movement of all wheat to the lakehead to tough and damp grades in view of the storage congestion in terminal elevators. The only other grain which may be moved, on the basis of specific orders from the board, is No. 1 feed and lower grades of barley and extra No. 1 feed and higher grades of oats. The lakehead terminal operators have given assurance that they will give Immediate unload to all car lots of tough and damp grain received.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I greatly appreciate that you have recognized me at this stage and thus offered me the occasion to bring certain conclusions to the remarks I had occasion to address to the house last evening. I realize that to be fair with everyone I should endeavour to be brief. I know the importance of the subject under debate, and I realize that other hon. members would also appreciate the opportunity to take part.
Last night I had occasion to impart certain information to the government to the effect that throughout Canada it is felt that this

present government, as far as laying down policies on defence and defence production are concerned, has failed not so much because of the merit of the decision taken a week ago but because the facts which have been brought out assure everyone in this country that there were delays and confusion which have made it apparent to the Canadian people that the policy laid down by this government is not the one which they had expected a government with the majority of this one would have brought down.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I intend to direct my attention particularly to the subamendment, and to this end I shall read the amendment to which the subamendment is appended. It was moved by the Leader of the Opposition and seconded by the hon. member for Laurier that:
This house regrets that the prolonged delay of the government in determining air defence policy and planning in co-operation with our allies is preventing the effective use of Canada's defence production facilities and manpower.
To which was added the subamendment:
-and is contributing to the erosion of Canadian sovereignty."
May I say to begin with that we welcome the opportunity of hearing the views of the opposition and of members supporting the government on this problem, which is one which transcends all other considerations. We welcome the opportunity of having the views of the hon. members on a matter that is exercising the minds of free men everywhere. Here in this house in a spirit of reasoned criticism it is proper that we should discuss this matter, which is being discussed everywhere in the free nations and in the assemblies of the free world.
I intend to refer to some recent debates that have taken place and in particular I shall refer to those that occurred in the United Kingdom. The question of defence was dealt with at great length in May of 1958; and only a few days ago, on February 25, 1959 there was a lengthy and complete discussion. It is appropriate that this question should be discussed, because since 1945 Canada has spent on its defences the sum of $15,700 million, exceeded only by the United States, the United Kingdom, France and West Germany. In other words during this period of time, following the experience at the United Nations meeting in San Francisco, the nations of the free world having concluded that the hopes there expressed would not be achieved because of the intransigent attitude of the U.S.S.R., the free world decided that its defences had to be maintained.
That view has been generally accepted. The Leader of the Opposition speaking on August 8 last admitted on that occasion that we- and I take it he meant Canada and the free

world-are now entering a new era in defence. That era of defence had been referred to by the Minister of National Defence, who preceded the Leader of the Opposition in the debate, as an era when the threat of the manned bomber is being supplemented by the threat of the missile. New methods and new plans are required to meet this problem.
In all the planning that has been done and in all the expenditures for defence that have been made since 1945 the unknown factor has been that we have not known the plans and intentions of the U.S.S.R. On the one hand the U.S.S.R. claims that it desires peace. In the last few days the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom during his stay in the U.S.S.R. has been met by the inconsistency of two attitudes, one the welcome attitude displayed from time to time and the other the attitude expressed in the truculent speech delivered by Khrushchev in which he banished any suggestion of the possibility of a foreign ministers' summit conference. Yesterday, however, in one of those kaleidoscopic changes that are characteristic of him Mr. Khrushchev agreed to the convening of such a conference which he himself only a few days before had ridiculed as something that under no circumstances he would accept.
It is difficult to understand in the light of these changing views what is the attitude of the U.S.S.R. The formal reply of the Soviet union following the harsh-sounding speech of Mr. Khrushchev on February 24 gives some new hope. It will be undergoing careful scrutiny in the NATO council tomorrow. All of us, I am sure, express the hope that the combination of the fair-minded approach of the western powers in their notes of February 16, together with what from preliminary press reports indicates may be a more reasonable response from the U.S.S.R. than we have encountered in recent months, may lead to a situation in which there could be a real lessening of tension and the dangers of the Berlin problem will be decreased.
We have had these intervals since 1945. On each occasion when there has been a softening of the attitude on the part of the Soviet union the free world has taken it to mean a change. Having regard to the terrible potentialities inherent in the fixing of May 27 as the date when the U.S.S.R. intends to set aside its pledged word, with all the awful consequences that may follow, all of us trust that there is realism in the hope that something may be achieved on this occasion that will bring about a lessening of tension.
In the finest traditions of British statesmanship the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom, without regard to the coldness of the response he received following Mr. Khrushchev's speech, stayed there believing that it
Defence Policy, Planning and Production is of the essence that the statesmen of the free world continue to do everything that is reasonable, in an endeavour through discussion and negotiation, to settle those issues that have separated us since 1945 or 1946. The unexpected and expected vagaries and changes in the attitude of the U.S.S.R. place the free world in the position of having to accept one of two alternatives. At all times we have to maintain the latest defences only to find out when there is no war that the weapons and defences have become obsolete. That has been the insurance we have continued to pay. On the other hand the course that some suggest is that we should spend a too-diminished amount or at too late a time.
In either case the course of statesmen in the free world is one of preparation in doubt, endeavouring to arrive at that course which is the best but at the same time realizing that in large measure the expenditures being made for defence may prove to have been expended on weapons that have become obsolete during the intervening years. While trying to anticipate the terrible instruments of the future we must at the same time maintain the closest vigilance in our endeavour to ascertain whether or not there is something that will bridge the chasm between the free world and the communist world.
In the intervening years the changes in the instruments of destruction have placed the instruments of offence far ahead of those of defence. In an age of atomic and hydrogen bombs, thermonuclear missiles and intercontinental ballistic missiles, mankind asks what the morrow will bring and what the future will be. Only last year the deputy chief of staff of the United States air force in charge of development said:
We should not regard control of the moon as the ultimate means of insuring peace among the earth nations. But the moon appears to be of such significance that we should not let another nation establish a military capability there ahead of us.
In other words, the limitless potentialities of the future which have come about through the intervening years with frightening change make the defence of today almost the weakness of tomorrow. In the last few days Rear Admiral John S. Thach, commander of the antisubmarine defence group in the United States, made this statement, again showing the terrible danger under which the free world finds itself:
A dozen Russian submarines packing Polaris (missiles) could wipe out 70 per cent of our economy in one surprise blow.
He was referring to the economy of the United States. To those who say that our defences are obsolete the answer of the free world is always this. It has been the answer in Britain; it has been the answer in the
1546	HOUSE OF
Defence Policy, Planning and Production United States, in France and in West Germany. What are the measures that we must take? Against what manner of attack are we to be prepared to defend ourselves? Because the great danger of today is that the theories and plans of defence today, in the light of the potentialities of tomorrow, become useless or innocuous.
On the other hand, we have to take into consideration the tremendous expenditures. The amount spent per year for defence of the world amounts to about $100 billion. We in Canada, a small country comparatively speaking as far as population is concerned, are in this position: we are situated between the U.S.S.R. and the United States of America. The question that we must ask ourselves is, what shall our future be? Shall we be rendered vulnerable to the instruments of mass destruction, against many of which there is no defence or, on the other hand, shall we find ourselves in the position that through overexpenditure, or through expending for those things which are not necessary, and in the light of experience cannot be justified to be continued-shall we by going on in that way face that which the U.S.S.R. and its leadership have said through the years will be the ultimate fate of the free world, economic bankruptcy?
It is in this spirit that I am going to discuss one or two matters today and in particular, as I said, the subamendment. I suggest that we leave aside the natural attitudes of political partisanship. I think that is the attitude of the house. Let us discuss in general some of the matters upon which we are agreed, and then endeavour to determine the course we should take.
All of us are agreed that an adequate defence is necessary. We are not agreed as to how it is to be obtained, for we do not know what is in the mind of the Kremlin. Some say it is to be a cold war of ideas. That is the point of view that is held in various countries in Asia; that the major responsibility of the free world is to assure that in the battlefield of ideas the idealism of free men and of democracy is of paramount importance.
On the other hand there are those who agree that the question of ideas and idealism has a large place, and I am of those who hold that opinion in part. I believe that we must convey a message to those uncomitted parts of the world which are today determining the course they shall follow. We must not lose sight of the necessity of placing before the peoples of those countries the idealism that is ours, the philosophy that we support and the general concept of the free world. It was in that spirit, following my trip to Asia, that I expressed the view that the time had come
[Mr. Dlefenbaker.l

for a declaration of the purposes of the democratic free world which are today to a considerable degree left for definition to the whims of its enemies. We need an understanding in this vital field of philosophy that is ours, and there is a compelling need for the free world to define its purposes, its principles and its ideals so they can fully be understood in every part of the world.
While material assistance to underdeveloped countries is most beneficial and Canada's contribution to that end has been a worthy one, material aid of itself is not sufficient. The time has come for us to explain what is our concept of freedom; for, after all, in the uncommitted countries of the world, the communist world is able to put forward its point of view and has successfully done so in many ways, while we in the free world have not been able to achieve the same degree of success. In other words, I suggest that there is no better way to explain freedom than in the spirit in which the Atlantic charter was declared during the darkest days of the war, and for the free world to reach a common basis for a declaration of freedom's creed. Then, having done so, let us give to the uncommitted world a solemn pledge of willingness to work with them for better economic conditions in which human dignity, equality and tolerance will be recognized and to which the personal freedoms-freedom of thought, expression, association and religion-will be dedicated in the struggle for man's hearts and minds.
During the last two days the Toronto Star in an article has come out in favour of action in that regard, action to assist the peoples of the uncommitted world. Indeed, it goes so far as to suggest that defence expenditures cannot defend the peoples of the free world. With that view I am not in accord, but I believe we must have the spiritual things properly brought to the attention of the uncommitted world. On the other hand we must preserve and maintain our defences so far as within us lies and in accordance with the needs and necessities of the present day.
I am not going into the detail which the Minister of National Defence and the Minister of Defence Production gave yesterday. I think both those contributions were outstanding. They placed before the people of Canada the picture of defence and also the action taken by this government to assure that we shall not be a silent and passive partner with the United States in defence on the North American continent.
I mentioned the discussions in the British House of Commons. Well, the last debate took place on February 25. There the opposition's attitude was the same as the opposition

here has evinced in the amendment. There the government was charged with failure to produce a coherent and effective defence policy, a charge almost identical in purport with the amendment moved here. But it is interesting to note that in the course of that debate the question as to the extent to which the United States of America was contributing and would have to contribute was referred to by the minister of defence, Right Hon. Mr. Sandys, in these words:
We believe that the Americans, who could afford it, were right in developing alternative deterrent weapons, in addition to the intercontinental land-based missiles into which they were putting their main effort.
He points out that the United States, being able to afford it, is taking certain stands. One of the most striking aspects of the trip I took was to see everywhere in the world the extent to which the United States, in the countries of the free world and in the uncommitted world, is taking over responsibilities that were formerly discharged for so long by Great Britain and the British Empire. It is taking them over because of the changing conditions and the economic results that have followed in the United States since 1914.
As far as Liberal policy in the United Kingdom is concerned, it was declared by Mr. Grimond, who said that Britain should not manufacture or maintain her own deterrent. The Liberal party believed that the deterrent should be held by the west and on behalf of the west as a whole, not by individual countries. The United States was at present so much the most powerful nuclear power that the nuclear deterrent must rest largely with it. Liberals were perfectly willing that Britain should make a contribution if it was wanted. They were not impressed by the arguments for mounting nuclear rockets on British soil, and shared the view that these might be distributed around the world.
In other words, disagreement takes place over there as it takes place here. What is the proper course to take? What are the instruments of today that will defend us tomorrow? Is there any missile defence? As far back as May 13, 1958 the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom warned that there is no known defence against ballistic missiles, and there is no sign of such a defence being developed. Authoritative sources have summarized British government policy on air defence along these lines. Britain does not have the financial or economic resources to develop planes that will be superseded in a few years by ballistic missiles, or may be obsolete by the time they go into production.
That is the attitude of this government. There is no purpose in manufacturing horse
Defence Policy, Planning and Production collars when horses no longer exist. Whatever the results may be, there can be no justification for defence procurement being used for any other purpose than the assurance of defence. Britain is concentrating her resources on building medium range rockets capable of carrying hydrogen warheads. No planes more advanced that the P-1 fighter or Victor and Vulcan will be designed. Production of all three planes is being pushed forward to tide Britain over the period until her air defences are taken over entirely by rockets.
What is our position in Canada? Some seem to have the view that we could be neutral in any war that may take place, neutral in the event that the United States was involved-or Britain, or France, or West Germany. There is no neutrality of that kind today. Our responsibilities under NATO, under the agreement entered into with the full cognizance and support of all members of parliament, will not allow any choice to be made in the future. There can be no academic debates in parliament or out of parliament on the question of whether or not we are automatically at war in the event that any of the nations in NATO are at war.
That is our position. There can be no other today in view of the international changes and the agreements entered into since 1948 and 1949. The defence of Canadian land, air and sea is a major if not the major strategic consideration on the North American continent and the most vital single item in the broad NATO strategy of early containment of the attack to protect the manoeuvrability of the main NATO weapon, the United States strategic air force. It was admitted quite fairly by the Leader of the Opposition that for Canada to have endeavoured to contribute a strategic air force would have been beyond the financial resources of the Canadian people.
Those are considerations to which we must have regard. Canada's part, as the Minister of National Defence has stated, is to protect Canada, to give warning to the United States air force, to the strategic air command. After all, whatever dialectical discussions there may be respecting the nature of NORAD, NORAD is indeed a part of NATO. NATO was advised of its formation. The NATO chart shows the Canada-United States planning group as reporting to the standing group. They act as a committee carrying out similar functions to those which would be carried out by the supreme commander, to use the words of the Minister of National Defence when giving evidence before the standing committee on estimates on June 10 last.
In other words, we here in Canada are in a position where our numbers do not permit

Defence Policy, Planning and Production us to provide for our defence by ourselves alone. I want to emphasize that very simple fact, a fact which seems to have been lost sight of during the course of this debate and on other occasions. I do so because the argument being used today is that we in Canada find ourselves as a satellite of the United States. Sir, there is co-operation. There must be co-operation. Without co-operation there is no survival for the people of either Canada or the United States.
Just a year ago the Leader of the Opposition said that a country of 17 million people cannot take over full responsibility for its own defence and that there were some things we cannot and should not do, that we could not afford the strategic bomber which is the principal deterrent. On the occasion when he spoke last year he also went on to point out some of the things which Canada should do, and I now wish to make reference to them. As found on page 3229 of Hansard for August 8, 1958, he said, and I remind him of this in view of his speech yesterday:
-Canada must have new and more powerful radar detection lines. It means new ground controls. It means participation in . . . semi-automatic ground environment. Surely it must also mean the introduction into our air defence forces of ground to air guided missiles such as the Bomarc, which we do not yet have but which in the future will perhaps become a major weapon in our air defence-
That was the suggestion of the Leader of the Opposition last August, and he pointed out at that time the difficulty of being able to predict the course of the U.S.S.R. and the needs for the future. He also went on to say that while the Bomarc missiles may not take the place of the manned interceptors at least for some time- I point out that he said this on August 8 last-they will certainly be supplementary to the manned interceptors.
Then he went on to say-almost in a prophetic way, because everyone was saying it at that time-that perhaps it would not be too long before the manned interceptor would be as obsolete as the old BE2C of the R.F.C. in which my hon. friend learned to fly. Then he said:	.
Are we going to go into the production and planning of these new planes and missiles, or should we not leave the production of this kind of weapon under the concept of division of tasks in a balanced collective defence strategy to the United States and concentrate our efforts in Canada, not exclusively but mostly, to ground environmental control and early warning systems against missile attack?
That is on page 3231 of Hansard for August 8, 1958. When they talk of the dangers of co-operation with the United States, this is what the hon. gentleman said, speaking in August last; that this is a situation in which

Canada is vitally and directly concerned, and with which we cannot deal except in the closest possible association with the United States.

Oh yes, there has been no change in that regard. Again, at page 3231 of Hansard to which I have referred, I find that my hon. friend said that Canada may have to wait before entering into the field of rocket and missile construction. Then he said, and now I quote:
Perhaps we will also have to adopt a system of priorities of a different kind from that which we have adopted in the past with regard to defence by confining our defence efforts, or at least devoting the major part of our defence efforts, to matters particularly concerned with questions of immediate interest to us such as radar defence, integration of ground equipment and ground control-
That was the statement of the hon. gentleman only a few short months ago and, I point out, prior to the time this government made its declaration with regard to the CF-105. In other words, following that debate in this house this government acted, apparently with unanimity in the light of the words of the Leader of the Opposition in determining that steps should be taken which would go in the direction which he himself had surveyed and indicated. Yet today, at a time when the people of North America and in every part of the free world are concerned as they have not been for a long time, if at any time since 1945, there are those who would create in the hearts and minds of Canadians a frenzied fear that co-operation with the United States means subordination.
It means nothing of the kind. When I hear hon. gentlemen opposite talk about subservience to the United States I ask them to look at the pages of history. What party was it that stood at all times for a Canada independent and within the commonwealth, or within the British empire as it was? During the years we took that stand, and that was our stand at all times; the necessity for Canadian sovereignty within Canada, and particularly maintaining a sense of international responsibility. The hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) was in this house and the hon. member for York East (Mr. McGregor) was in this house in the days when the party opposite sat over here and said, do not take any stand against the United States; do not do anything that might annoy them. Now they have suddenly become the champions of Canadian sovereignty. What about the stand taken for years and years that you should not at any time stand up for an assurance of equality?

I have always been very strongly Canadian, and I say this, sir. If anyone endeavours to suggest to me and give the Canadian people the idea that joining together for our salvation and survival, whereby each recognizes that the other is a partner-which is the only sensible way to survive-means that we are turning over this country to the United States and allowing it to be dominated by the United States, then I say that suggestion is not in keeping with the seriousness of the situation with which we are faced. I say it is the best way that we can look forward to tomorrow with a reasonable degree of hope.
Yes, they appear to fear the erosion of Canadian sovereignty. Is there any loss of sovereignty by reason of the fact that we fail to continue to produce an aircraft whose outermost range at subsonic speed is not more than 500 miles and at supersonic speed is about three-quarters of that distance? Let us face the situation as we see it. Let me assure the house and the country that this government has been solicitous for and outspoken against anything in the nature of an invasion of Canadian rights since we took power.
As a matter of fact we have been pictured as being anti-American, at least I have. However, that is not true, because I am pro-Canadian. We believe that Canadian sovereignty must be maintained; that is of the essence. Is there any loss of sovereignty in the United Kingdom? Have they ever talked such nonsense over there, even with United States troops on their soil from time to time, and with United States defence establishments there? Have the other NATO countries ever talked in this way? Is there any subordination of sovereignty there? This is the only course. It would be very wonderful for Canada to say, all alone, "Here we are, sovereign in our own domaine alone". There is no sovereignty, Mr. Speaker, without survival; that is the essence of the course we have taken. There is assurance that our northern areas shall be preserved.
My hon. friends opposite talk about sovereignty and express in lachrymose terms their feelings over the loss of sovereignty. What government was it that brought back to Canada sovereignty over the D.E.W. line? It was the government of today. My hon. friends opposite; did they ever talk about the loss of sovereignty when they allowed the United States to build these vast establishments in Canada, on Canadian soil? Were they shocked, as they pretend to be now, by the division of responsibility and the division of cost as between Canada and 66968-9-99
Defence Policy, Planning and Production the United States when the mid-Canada line and the Pinetree line were built? Let us view this matter with objectivity and without emotional inaccuracies such as the hon. gentleman and those associated with him opposite have shown in the last few days. I believe that the United States must be made to realize, and I welcome the fact that hon. gentlemen opposite have joined with us in this regard, that Canada and the United States are partners. We demand as of right the exercise of those things which are incidental to the fair and proper discharge of a partnership.
That brings me to this question. How often have gentlemen opposite laughed when we talked of plans for northern development to secure the northern areas for Canada so that they would not be lost. In the last few weeks something of that development plan which was scoffed at, the design of which was to improve the economic future of Canada and also preserve those areas for our defence, has been shown to be achieving fruition in the events which have taken place in connection with those vast mineral and oil areas which are today being taken up. Having said that, may I now say I believe most strongly that we intend to continue to assert unswervingly that we shall have for Canada a fair, full and equal participation in all decisions which go to our common defence. We want the assurance, too, that defence dollars will be spent in Canada in a fair and proper division. Those assurances we have asked for. Those assurances we have not achieved as yet in their entirety; but certainly the events of the last year indicate that as a result of the stand we took a committee has been set up by the United States congress, as well as a committee of ministers. Meetings of those committees are designed to assure that degree of consideration which each partner has the right to demand from the other.
Then we are accused of having contributed to the erosion of Canadian sovereignty. That sovereignty, as I see it, has two aspects: The maintenance of the sovereignty within the framework of our NATO defence, and offensively it consists of seizing the opportunities to maintain and assure our de facto sovereignty over the whole northern area. Do United States bases in Canada derogate from Canada? Is Newfoundland a subject province because it has one or more United States bases there? Those bases are of essence of survival and today maintain the bulwark of our eastern and Atlantic defences. Surely we should not endeavour to fan the fires of fear in the hearts of Canadians when co-operation such as is taking place is of the essence for our survival. The people who say that we

Defence Policy, Planning and Production raise these fears today only a few years ago said "Do not provoke the United States. Do not raise any objections." From the time this government assumed power we have pressed, we have contended, and in many cases we have secured what we were asking for, not always in whole but certainly in part; and I am going to come in a minute to what the hon. gentleman himself said in this regard.
As far as NATO and our continental defences are concerned, we take the stand-we have no reason to take other-that our actions within the continental context of North America are all within the contemplation of NATO. All of them have the approval of the NATO organization. I think one of the better editorials on this question of sovereignty was that in the Toronto Telegram of February 24, when it said this:
The charge that cancellation of the production contract for Arrow aircraft involves any degree of surrender of Canadian sovereignty is wholly wrong. It is farfetched beyond the limits of common sense, for the Arrow decision is, in fact, an exercise of independence by Canada without precedent in the history of our military alliance with the United States, which dates from 1940.
Then it goes on to say, however:
Canadian security demands co-operation with the United States, and Canada co-operates in continental defence for its own benefit, and it is wise to recognize that the same motives apply in Washington.
I underline the next portion of it because this represents the facts as they are:
The only pressure upon the Canadian government in deciding to abandon the Arrow was to serve the best interests of Canada and its defence needs. There is no suggestion of outside pressure, no reason to argue that Canadian sovereignty has been in any way prejudiced.
Then it went on to deal with the question to which I now want to refer, the question of production. That was dealt with at length by both hon. gentlemen, and there are only one or two matters I will refer to in that connection. However, we have been speaking of the economic co-operation agreement between Canada and the United States, which is dated October 26, 1950. This document, which all hon. members have, sets forth the principles for economic co-operation. The arrangements worked out under the Hyde Park agreement proved so successful that when international conditions again appeared threatening the joint United States-Canada industrial mobilization planning committee was established on April 12, 1949, to make plans in case joint action should again become necessary. The document goes on to say:
It is agreed, therefore, that our two governments shall co-operate in all respects practicable, and to the extent of their respective executive powers, to the end that the economic efforts of the two countries be co-ordinated for the common
[Mr. Diefenbaker.l
defence and that the production and resources of both countries be used for the best combined results.
Then it sets out the principles which are established for the purpose of facilitating these objectives:
-the two countries shall develop a co-ordinated program of requirements, production, and procurement.
What else have we done but carry out in that particular-I will deal with this later -the agreement entered into by the government of which the hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) was a member? Then, secondly:
To this end, the two countries shall, as it becomes necessary, institute co-ordinated controls over the distribution of scarce war materials and supplies ... To the extent possible, there shall be consultation to this end prior to the institution of any system of controls in either country which affects the other.
In order to facilitate essential production, the technical knowledge and productive skills involved in such production within both countries shall, where feasible, be freely exchanged.
Barriers which impede the flow between Canada and the United States of goods essential for the common defence effort should be removed as far as possible.
I point out that oil was mentioned today, as was the protest that we made. When the hon. gentleman opposite was among those formerly in power that particular provision was evaded, or avoided in operation, by the United States. I shall say no more at this time except to express the purpose of this government. Our purpose is to ensure that in no partisan way Canada will have that defence which her financial situation will permit, her international responsibilities demand and which co-operation and partnership should ensure. I suggest to my hon. friends opposite that it is really nonsense to endeavour to lead the Canadian people to believe that in following his suggestions with respect to the Sage and the Bomarc we would be following a proper course for Canada. Having regard to the seriousness of the awful potentialities inherent in the defence policy of a nation this government will follow a course of national survival -and I emphasize national survival-that will assure our national sovereignty and the attainment of our national destiny.
That is the course we have taken. I will not say we shall always be right because since 1945 no government, no minister of national defence and no prime minister in any of the countries of the free world that I know of has been able to look ahead and say, "this will be the course." The munitions planned in 1947, 1948, 1949 and 1950 have had to be discarded. The aircraft of that day which were regarded as the ultimate in all perfections have become obsolete. What we have tried to do and what our plan remains is to take the role of full partnership and responsibility here in Canada and to work with the United States whose strategic air command represents the only hope we have of a deterrent. We intend to work with the United States without in any way surrendering our sovereignty. We will work with the United States in the same way as the United States and Canada work with all the other countries of NATO on the continent of Europe to the end that in a spirit of unity and a common dedication of purpose we shall be able to assure to this and future generations that freedom which we inherited.

Many Avro workers took him at his word and made plans and personal commitments on that basis because they felt

that they could rely on their jobs and their security at least until March 31, but they were wrong; they had been let down. To paraphrase many of the speeches made on the other side of the house during an earlier debate some years ago, they were sold down the river.
Well, sir, the Prime Minister did not anticipate the extent of the consequences of the short-circuit which he caused by pulling the switch on Friday morning. He seemed to be hurt as well as surprised by the fact that the company laid off all of its hourly and weekly paid employees forthwith. He should not have been surprised and he had no reason to feel hurt because the company just did as ordered by his own defence production department, and I quote:
You shall cease all work immediately, terminate subcontracts and orders, place no further subcontracts or orders and instruct all your subcontractors and suppliers to take similar action.
"Immediately", the telegram says, at once, without delay. Last Monday afternoon we criticized the government for the way in which it had handled this whole affair. We considered it clumsy, inept and incompetent. We are now convinced that we were correct in that judgment.
The Prime Minister entered the debate and made his speech which was described by several newspaper people as one of his finest. He had made his case, with the assistance of innumerable newspaper clippings that the company should have known last September what the fate of the Arrow was and that the contract would inevitably be cancelled. He rose to new heights of oratory, and one member of the press gallery said that he should be given a clean bill of health. Before agreeing with this, Mr. Speaker, it is necessary to consider his responsibility in this matter.
Let us assume that the Prime Minister was correct in his opinion and that he had made the case that the company should have known since last September that the contract was to be cancelled. If he was correct and the company should have known, then the Prime Minister must have known. Surely that much logic is not unreasonable. If the Prime Minister had his mind made up last September and the decision was a military one as he asserted, he should have cancelled the project then and saved Canadian taxpayers $100 million. The only possible excuse under the circumstances for delaying the decision to February, 1959 would be the use of the intervening five months to find some alternative to keep the scientific, engineering and manpower potential of the plant usefully employed. That was not done.
Defence Policy, Planning and Production
So the decision was announced abruptly and without any apparent solution being put forward by the government. Actually the search for an alternative plan should have started long before last September. In the light of what the Prime Minister and the Minister of National Defence have told us during this debate and a week ago yesterday, they knew of these great, far-reaching world events. They knew they might have to change their course of procedure. They knew that great things were in the offing and they should at that time have considered the possibility that they might later cancel the Arrow contract and what that would mean to Canadian defence, what it would mean to Canadians as individuals and what they would do in the event that the contract was cancelled. But apparently nothing was considered before last September.
It was not enough to send teams to the United States and to the United Kingdom to visit plants and to explore the possibility of getting some part of the production of these plants for Canadian factories. Surely, Mr. Speaker, it could not be reasonably expected that plants in the United Kingdom and the United States would give up some portion of their contracts when there is already considerable unemployment in those countries. Surely this is a matter which has to be settled at the ministerial level or even at the prime ministerial level. It is not a matter which can be settled by teams visiting plants in other countries, necessary though that may have been for purposes of reconnaissance. Production sharing is something which can only be determined at the highest governmental level and it is something to which the government should have applied itself.
In his speech last Monday the Prime Minister mentioned his world tour. We had no objection to his making that trip. As a matter of fact, we were pleased that he should travel around the world, visit various countries and find out at first hand how highly Canada is regarded in all the countries of the world, a condition that came about under the previous administration and largely through the good offices of the present Leader of the Opposition. We had no objection, as I said, to the Prime Minister taking that trip. What we did and do object to is the fact that before the Prime Minister went on the trip he did not make some of the important decisions facing the country at that time, decisions which would have such a great influence on the future of Canadians generally and which were left in abeyance while he was away. The people left in charge either were not competent or not able to deal with

One place the Prime Minister did not visit was Washington, and that is one place where we think he should have gone. We think he should have gone to Washington and stayed there until he had come to some satisfactory agreement with the government of the United States. He should not have taken any fast brush-off. He should have sat down with his counterpart in the United States and the officials there and worked out some satisfactory system for the mutual defence of the North American continent and for production sharing between our two countries, including sufficient developmental work for Canadian scientists, engineers and our creative capacity here. The statement of the Minister of National Defence yesterday afternoon was not very reassuring. In every debate there seems to be some ludicrous inference. In this debate the most incredible inference is the suggestion that whereas the CF-100 interceptor is not obsolete, the CF-105 is and that is the reason it is not being put into squadron service.
The minister told us the CF-100 would not be obsolete so long as Russian bombers existed. This statement is in Hansard for yesterday in case the Prime Minister wishes to find it. So long as there is a Russian bomber capable of coming here and back, the minister said, or even capable of coming one way we must keep our CF-lOO's and Bomarcs. This suggestion should not be allowed to mislead the Canadian people. The CF-100 Mark V is not now capable of dealing with the latest Russian bombers. In not too many months, if the Russian bombers carry air-to-air guided missiles, the CF-100 will be nothing but a sitting duck. At such a time the whole fleet, with its present armaments, might just as well be put in moth balls. We will then be completely defenceless against both manned bombers and missiles. Two weeks ago we were well on the road to having at least some defence against the former, but now we have decided to ignore both.
If, as the minister said, there is a continuing threat against the United Kingdom from the manned bomber we might expect there would be a similar threat against the North American continent. Indeed, the minister
Defence Policy, Planning and Production reinforced this view with a statement yesterday when he said that the reason we are introducing Bomarcs, just as the United States is, and are keeping our interceptor squadrons in service is that if we are attacked the Russians would use, in addition to the missiles that they have available, such aircraft as they could reasonably divert from other targets, and which might be used against secondary targets. Surely, some of our Canadian targets would qualify as secondary targets.
The United States Bomarc line, which includes two stations to be built in Canada, is not designed for the defence of Canada. It is designed for the defence of the United States and that, as the minister well knows, is the reason it is intended to stretch across the northernmost part of the United States. The only reason we have two stations is that the southern parts of Ontario and Quebec jut down below the 49th parallel, and the line cuts right through. There was a discussion earlier, before this government took office, of the possibility of moving the whole line 300 or 400 miles farther north in order that it might play some part in the protection of Canada. Surely that would have been something the government might have considered and might have pressed on the United States so that we would have, in fact, some defence for our western Canadian cities. Then, too, there would have been some defence against bombers before they got close enough to float guided missiles into our Canadian targets, and any planes knocked down by the United States Bomarc squadrons would fall in less populated areas rather than over our southern towns and cities.

The minister told us yesterday very gravely that if we let our armour down, and then he paused before continuing as if to say that the government would be held

Defence Policy, Planning and Production responsible, but instead he said that there might not be many left to blame. That is precisely what we are doing. We are letting our armour down. We have decided, for the moment at least, to pursue a course of no defence at all. The United States Bomarc stations below the 49th parallel will not protect our western cities from air-to-ground missiles, notwithstanding the minister's assurance. The minister concluded by saying that in respect of national defence policy, there was no confusion. Well, certainly not, Mr. Speaker, because there is no policy and it is axiomatic if there is no policy there is no confusion. However, the Canadian people may be forgiven for being somewhat confused.
The Prime Minister, during a visit to Toronto in 1957, condemned as unjust and untrue propaganda a story that the Conservatives, if elected, would reduce military power. He went on to say that this report was false in every particular and had no basis in fact.

It is from the report in the Toronto Star of May, 1957, following a meeting in Toronto. The Prime Minister seemed to be more aware of the need then than he is now or than he has been since he took office. The defence estimates for 1959-60, including mutual aid, are reduced by some $182.4 million. Our share of the burden of defence, already less than some of our allies are called upon to bear, is being reduced. We are, apparently, going to be content to ride on the back of the United States people, and lose our right to a strong voice on the problems of joint concern.
This is a very grave situation. One thing that has resulted from the debates of last week is that the government has given us much more information than previously, and I think that is good. It gives the public and members of parliament a chance to consider defence in the light of this additional information which was very much needed.
Now, important as the Avro decision is, it is but a part of the greater picture, both of military defence and defence against encroaching ideologies. There are hundreds of thousands of Canadians from coast to coast who have been out of work for weeks and months. They, too, have an urgent requirement, the requirement of useful employment to provide themselves with a living and a chance to contribute their share to the collective strength of the Canadian nation.
To sum up, Mr. Speaker, I should like to come back to our original contention. We turn to the central tragedy of the whole situation. First, we are to have no defence
[Mr. Hellyer.1
except that which the United States chooses to give us. We should have obtained their co-operation instead of just leaving it to them. Incidentally, the Prime Minister said that without co-operation there cannot be survival either for Canada or the United States. Fair, full and equal decisions in all matters concerning common defence, he said, must be ours. We must join together for common survival. Well, that is right, Mr. Speaker. We must join together, but joining together with the United States for survival should not place this country in the position in which we find ourselves under the present government. We do not have the joining together of a marriage as partners but rather a joining together in a similar way to that in which Jonah joined the whale.
Secondly, we have more unemployment to add to that already very vexatious problem. Thirdly, we have dissipated much of the potential of providing ourselves with any future defence. This is not Canada's destiny as outlined to us by the Prime Minister. In the statement of the Prime Minister last Monday he blamed the military decision on the chiefs of staff and the mass lay-offs on the company. This is getting to be a habit. He blames the deficit on the Liberals, the unemployment on the international situation, the military decision to cancel the Arrow on the chiefs of staff, and the mass lay-offs on the company. One might be forgiven for wondering if it is always true-

Mr. Speaker, I propose to take just a few minutes of the time of the house to deal with an area which has been, to some extent, covered, but after the third day of debate on this subject it is difficult not to be repetitious. I do not propose to comment on the hon. gentleman's remarks or his address, but he does speak of confusion. If ever we listened to a confused contribution, it was indeed his.
This attempt by the opposition, who live in two worlds, to offer a series of contradictions one after another was clearly nailed to the cross by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) when he read back the remarks of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson). The people of Canada can judge fairly whether the opposition desire to make a constructive contribution to this defence debate or rather are merely taking the position of someone who has been struck down in a motor accident and, looking through the bandages in his bed, just argues that he really did have the right of way after all. I suggest, that the several

speeches we have heard today which combine in an attempt, first of all, to suggest that we should live beyond our means with equipment which is not suitable for our defence, and, secondly, to create animosities with our partner, the United States, are indeed of great disservice to this country and to this country's defence program.
We have heard much of this question of sovereignty as though it were something the opposition had all of a sudden just discovered. The objective of co-operation with the United States in both peace and wartime has been something which we desired and have worked for for many years. Those in this house who served overseas well remember the days when our fighter squadrons accompanied many of the U.S. B-17 squadrons when they took part in actions which were an integral part of defence under a United States general. They will remember the work which our transport command did in carrying services and supplies in their behalf. They will remember the bomber units which together functioned as an integral part of the defence of Europe, and there was never any question of sovereignty at that time. We were operating as partners in defence of a country, and in opposition to a common foe. It will be said today, of course, by those in opposition that that was in wartime. I suggest that that is no argument. It is purely academic, because today, with the emergency of the situation which we see in front of us, we cannot afford to sit down and disagree on what is going to be a Canadian proportion or a United States part of an operation: We must work it out as a joint enterprise as we did in two great wars.
Let us look at past history for just a moment where our co-operation in more recent times has also been well established. It has been said in this house by the Prime Minister -I am sure there will be no opposition to this sentiment-that the United States strategic air command has to a very substantial degree been the one dominant factor which has maintained peace in the world over the last few years. This is a body whose striking force and retaliatory power has made war so terrible that it has maintained the peace. This is the first and foremost defence against war, and on the basis of determining future policy we entered into an agreement with the United States which we know as NORAD. I do not intend to repeat the arguments which have taken place in this house other than to say that there was certainly no reticence on behalf of the opposition as to the need for an agreement, but I would comment on the remarks of the Leader of the Opposition who spoke of the fact that there had been a great deal of co-operation prior to the NORAD agreement. I suggest that that is not the
Defence Policy, Planning and Production whole case. There was a loose arrangement, but it was the NORAD agreement that laid the basis on which this partnership was to be formed. Now we find that we are in a closely knit defence alliance, one which is still providing us with the same measure and degree of efficiency of operation and, perhaps more important, an understanding in the event of an emergency, as to how best we can defend not just Canada but the continent as a whole.
I am going to make a reference to the Avro Arrow program and remind those gentlemen who were members of the estimates committee of a particular recommendation which we made when we were discussing the need, first of all, to determine whether we would be able to sell a particular weapon or ao it alone on any particular weapon program. May I quote from the recommendation on page 590 of the final report of this committee. It says this:
-with respect to further development of this portion of the defence program . . . and in view of the heavy financial burden, the committee does express its concern in the government entering into any subsequent weapon program of this magnitude without first negotiating for some cost-sharing agreement with either NATO member countries or the U.S.A. under the NORAD agreement.
I remind the house that it was in 1952 that this particular undertaking, the Arrow program, was first considered. The Leader of the Opposition suggested that some efforts were made to sell the Arrow, and he quoted from the minister's comments. He asked why it was not possible after this aircraft had reached the pre-production stage to sell it to the United States. Mr. Speaker, there is not that difference between 1951 and 1958 that the Leader of the Opposition would have you believe. First of all, I suggest that if there were any question about who had the first reason to sell this aircraft, it should have been raised in the initial stage when it was designed and we decided to proceed with it. Some four years later we find that the aircraft in its pre-production stage was ready to take its first flight, and we discover it is very limited in the field of defence to which it can make any useful contribution. Of course, the United States at this late date would be expected to say that this does not fit into the defence plans for this continent, and consequently it becomes impossible some four years later to sell it.
To return to this question of whether or not the government should have made its decision six or eight months earlier, I remind hon. members that first of all we made a contribution of $174 million toward the development of this aircraft in the course of the last session. It seems inconceivable to

Defence Policy, Planning and Production me that at this stage, having paid for 36 pre-production models we should turn around and cancel this aircraft before we knew what the flight characteristics were. At that point only four had been tested. As I say, it seems inconceivable that having made the basic payment we should cancel the project without knowing what the limitations and capabilities of the aircraft were.
And now I should like to refute suggestions which have been made in some quarters with regard to the morale of the Royal Canadian Air Force. I have heard it said in this house that morale has sunk to a low point because of the cancellation of this one airplane. Like many others in this house, I have been associated for some years with this corps, and I suggest it is an insult to the intelligence of these men to say that because the Arrow does not fit into a defence program the morale of an extremely fine fighting force will be lowered. The impression has been created by some speakers that this is the end of the air force. The suggestion has been made that the force has no further objective. Nothing could be further from the truth. As hon. members know, the R.C.A.F. is maintaining a very extensive maritime command, a very large transport command and an active training command. In addition, an important contribution has been made to the training of air cadets not only within the framework of NATO but within the context of other alliances. Besides all this we are, of course, maintaining 12 squadrons abroad.
I suggest, also, that during the course of this debate on national defence many hon. members have overlooked another factor of great importance, and I refer particularly to one statement made by the Prime Minister as reported on page 122 of Hansard for February 20, which reads:
The Minister of National Defence and the chiefs of staff are now engaged in further studies of the various alternatives for the improvement of our defences.
It is quite obvious that some hon. members have completely lost sight of this area of the subject. It has been suggested that because we have cancelled one aircraft we are completely defenseless. It was suggested by the hon. member who has just resumed his seat that the CF-100 is not competent to continue to perform the task for which it has been well suited for many years.
I would point out that we should not lose sight of the fact that the subject of national defence is one which has more than one aspect and that there are many important areas which should be discussed at the present time. If we are going to take an unrealistic view of our problems and develop


certain sections of our defence arrangements without any recognition of changing circumstances, it would mean that a defence budget of $1,700 million would not pay for even a portion of our requirements. What we must do, and what we have done in the dropping of the Arrow program is recognize that we must spend our money in the direction in which it will produce best results, and cut our coats according to our cloth. We should not involve ourselves in defence measures which would have only a limited application, but must recognize the necessity for integrating our plans with those of the United States.
I hope to have an opportunity at a later date to discuss some of the military aspects of our national defence program, but I should like at this point to read a section of a speech which was made by the chief of the air staff at Montebello on Thursday, February 5. In the course of the speech Air Marshal Hugh Campbell said:
In air defence, for example, we have been given the green light on two half-squadrons of Bomarc, one Sage sector and extended radar coverage. The first two of these programs call for heavy training schedules and will require substantial numbers of men to operate the equipment. The extended radar coverage to be provided by raising the capability of our Pinetree radars and by installing two new heavy radars and several gap fillers in northern Quebec and Ontario will also affect our manpower.
What is much more important, however, is the increased capacity that all three programs will give us to deal with the airborne threat to North America. This threat is real-make no mistake about it-and we must be able to deal with it. The success of Sage and Bomarc installations in the United States is indeed heartening. We know that the Bomarc, operating in its Sage environment will greatly augment our air defences.
Here is a professional soldier, the senior Canadian air officer, clearly stating the advantages to be obtained from the type of defence which this government is setting up. I suggest that when those who have no particular knowledge of this subject disagree with an opinion stated by the chief of the air staff, it then becomes contrary to the views of those who are best able, through experience to speak on this subject.
I would close on the note on which I began by suggesting that this is hardly the time to concern ourselves to the extent we have about questions of sovereignty when our national survival should be our supreme consideration. Canadian sovereignty is being protected, as the Prime Minister has made clear. The present debate gives the house an opportunity to realize that we are in a very precarious position and that we must therefore co-operate with our United States partners in every way in order to provide the best defence possible for Canada, and thus be able to be in a position for many years to

continue to give our co-operative defence with that country. I hope that when this debate is concluded the impression will not be left abroad that we have taken time in this house to argue, to the exclusion of everything else, matters to which the Canadian public has for years given its approval. The public realizes that national defence is something which has to be co-ordinated, and that is the action we have taken.

In the course of this debate speakers for the government and speakers on the opposition side as well seem, equally, to have overlooked the effect of the decision which the government has taken upon the workers involved in the aircraft industry. I believe that this question is of importance for the 14,000 people who have been laid off as the result of the government's decision, and that their fate is something which should commend itself to all hon. members of this house.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) when speaking the other day attacked the company severely for having discharged its employees immediately on receipt of the telegram saying that the CF-105 contract was being terminated. He made a big point of saying that it was not necessary for the company to discharge all its employees on receipt of this telegram. He must have been referring only to the 3,000 who are now back at work, because nothing the Prime Minister has said would suggest that the company should have endeavoured to retain 14,000 men in employment.
The question arises as to what the government's policy shall be as to employment for the men and women in this industry who are now out of work. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) touched upon this question on Friday, February 27, when he told the house that a co-operative arrangement had been worked out between the government and Avro to provide for the continued employment of a certain technical group but when the minister made this statement he also said it was the hope that the action being taken by the government would bring employment in the industry up to some 3,000. In view of the action of the government and of the company the best the minister was able to say to the house was that 3,000 might be employed in the industry. The head of the machinists' union upon learning of this statement said that in his opinion instead of putting some 1,000 people back to work the probability was that only some 250 would be employed by this means.
The company itself because of the action it has taken must bear some responsibility for the employment of 11,000 persons in this
Defence Policy, Planning and Production industry. But even if the industry had not had a government contract surely it is a part of government responsibility to provide employment opportunities for the people of this country. The government definitely has a responsibility and I believe the company also has a responsibility not only to its employees as such and because its employees have given the company good service for a long period of time but I feel it has a particular obligation because of the huge value of the contracts received from the Canadian government over a good many years. As a matter of fact, this company has been nurtured on government contracts. The information I have is that up to the end of March 1958, A. V. Roe and its subsidiaries had obtained the staggering total of $1,120 million in defence contracts with additional hundreds of millions to come after that date.

I do not have those figures. These figures are for the company and its subsidiaries but it would be hundreds of millions of dollars, of course, because the value of the CF-105 contract itself was over $300 million. The company has done very well over the years. In the past it has bought all the stock of Canadian Car and Foundry Company with assets of more than $40 million, it has purchased a controlling interest in Dominion Steel and Coal Corporation with assets of more than $150 million and in addition to that it obtained a large interest in Algoma Steel with assets of another $140 million. The company has extended its operations and I submit it has a duty to its employees. The record of this company as far as its employees in its subsidiaries are concerned leaves a great deal to be desired. In Nova Scotia, Dosco has turned out thousands of workers from the coal mines and Canadian Car Company Limited has discharged many of its employees. I believe it is fair to ask if this company has a good labour record. That does not in any way detract from the necessity of this government taking action to see that employment opportunities are provided for these 11,000 workers as well as other workers across the country who require employment.
In this matter I would suggest a committee of this house should be established. Perhaps it should be a small one. The committee could have come before it witnesses from Avro, the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Pearkes), the Minister of Defence Production (Mr. O'Hurley), the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) and other ministers who have an interest in this problem. As a parliament let us see whether we can study this problem
