And omitted my hon. friend? The Prime Minister made a long and energetic speech this afternoon. While he seemed to direct almost the whole of his attack at the official opposition I noticed the frequent reference he made to the subject matter of the subamendment in which it is charged that the action of the government contributes to the erosion of Canadian sovereignty. That is the question to which the Prime Minister directed much of his attention and quite properly so. That is a question that is worrying the Prime Minister. There is perhaps nobody in Canada who is better qualified to speak on this subject in view of the Prime Minister's many statements in the past than is that hon. gentleman himself.
What is the record of this government in terms of protecting Canadian sovereignty? Is it any better than the record of the previous administration? We had a case raised before the last election. The Ford Motor Company of Canada lost the opportunity of making sales of automobiles to China because of a law in the United States affecting its parent company and the parent company refused it the opportunity to make such sales. Can that company make that kind of sale today? Perhaps a better question would be this: would that company make that kind of sale today? I do not think there is any certainty that Canada has sufficient sovereignty as far as the automobile industry is concerned to have made available to it markets in China if such markets were available.
Is the China market available for the Canadian rubber belting industry? A case was brought before the house a few weeks ago by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch). Evidence was placed on the record that the Goodrich company in the United States refused to allow the Canadian subsidiary to sell rubber belting to China. I asked the government how its record of protecting Canadian sovereignty compares with the record of the previous government? Oh, I will admit that more statements and more noise have been made on the subject but I suggest the results have not been any more substantial.
When he was in the opposition the Prime Minister used to complain about the United States program for the export of agricultural


products and he asked the Liberal government of that day to take action. What action is this government taking on this important question, I ask, when all commentators say that the United States is embarking on a program to dispose of agricultural surpluses that will be a more far-reaching program than any it has been engaged upon in the past.
What is the attitude of the United States government toward the CF-105? Speaking on this question on February 23, the Minister of National Defence, as reported at page 1279 of Hansard, said:
The United States air force officers . . . are of the opinion that the F-106 fulfils their requirements rather better than the CF-105, and the F-106 would be a great deal cheaper for them than the CF-105. Prior to about 1956 we had not been aware of the fact that the United States government were going into the production of an aircraft similar to our CF-105. So again it was emphasized that the program which was being developed on the CF-105 could be altered, or if necessary abandoned, at any time.
Back in 1956, when Canada had begun the production of the CF-105, the United States, with no consideration for Canada's plants and facilities, had embarked on the production of their own F-106. I would suggest that at that time the United States showed a callous disregard for Canada which w*as then a part of a North American partnership, as she is today. That disregard for Canada's interests, that inability to take Canada as a full partner, has continued since that time. We have other instances in this session already of where Canada's sovereignty has been threatened. We have the instance of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) making a pilgrimage to Washington to discuss this very question. Was this government able to protect Canadian sovereignty on this trip? I do not think it is at all certain because in reporting to the house on this question, at page 619 of Hansard, the Minister of Justice had this to say:
It should he realized that there was revealed in the course of these discussions, a wide divergence between our two views as to what amounts to an infringement of sovereignty and as to the restraint which one country should exercise in seeking decrees from its own courts when those decrees may have effects within another country. Until there is a satisfactory reconciliation of views on these points there can be no guarantee that causes for complaint will not arise again.
There is the statement of the Minister of Justice after his return from Washington that this whole question of infringement of Canadian sovereignty has not been solved and that there is no assurance whatsoever that the United States will not continue such an infringement of Canadian sovereignty in the future. That is why we in this group have moved the amendment saying that the policy

of this government in relation to the United States and in relation to defence "is contributing to the erosion of Canadian sovereignty".
We believe in adequate defence; we believe that our defence forces should be as effective as possible; we believe that instead of Canada having this bilateral arrangement with the United States, which is called NORAD, we should have placed NORAD under the NATO command, and that the defence of North America should directly have been the responsibility of NATO. If that were done I believe that Canada's sovereignty would have been better protected; because if Canada could sit down with the United States to discuss this matter along with other members of the NATO alliance we feel that the United States, because of our then associated strength, would have to give much greater weight to the representations that we make. We think that the Canadian government surrendered a good deal of Canadian sovereignty when it went into the NORAD agreement, as it did, without making NORAD subject to the NATO command. We say that Canada's sovereignty is being eroded today and I hope that when the vote is taken, in the light of statements that have been made in the past by the members of the official opposition and in the light of their own amendment, they will find it possible to vote for the subamendment that we have moved and express at least to that extent what I believe to be of very great concern to Canadians generally, namely that under this government there has been a continuation of the erosion of Canadian sovereignty.

maintopic: DEFENCE POLICY, DEFENCE PLANNING, DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: Because of the former understanding I appreciate the ruling you have made but I should like to move that the Leader of the Opposition be now heard.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: DEFENCE POLICY, DEFENCE PLANNING, DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this is a peculiar sort of game we are up against today. Here we have this real combination working again. Now, the debate has gone backwards and forwards-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: DEFENCE POLICY, DEFENCE PLANNING, DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: I am sorry; this is not a debatable motion. Is there a seconder for the motion? The hon. member for Rosedale.

maintopic: DEFENCE POLICY, DEFENCE PLANNING, DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we have had another exhibition today of the co-operation which exists between the two great opposition parties.

maintopic: DEFENCE POLICY, DEFENCE PLANNING, DEFENCE PRODUCTION

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: DEFENCE POLICY, DEFENCE PLANNING, DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: He was out of order to refer to what had transpired immediately prior to the hon. member taking the floor. That having been settled and decided let us continue.

maintopic: DEFENCE POLICY, DEFENCE PLANNING, DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have heard a great deal during this debate about the amendment, but not a great deal has been

Defence Policy, Planning and Production directed to the actual wording of the amendment that the government is preventing the effective use of Canada's defence production facilities and manpower. I have been amazed at the hon. member for Assiniboia, (Mr. Argue), in speaking to the amendment, saying that the government was aiding and contributing to the erosion of Canadian sovereignty. It appears that the hon. member for Assiniboia could not have been in the house during the Prime Minister's address because not only did he make one point but 10 points to indicate that not only has there been no erosion but that Canadian sovereignty has been enhanced greatly by the contribution of this government over the past two years.
May I say that for a long time now I have been examining the facilities of the Canadian government for defence production. What is the largest facility? It is A. V. Roe Canada Limited. Yet nobody has outlined, or sought to outline, the background, the experience and the capacities of this organization. The hon. member for Trinity has spoken from day to day as if he were almost one of that organization, so enthusiastic has he been in its support. Nevertheless I decided to do some research into Avro and come up with an answer to its present plight.

maintopic: DEFENCE POLICY, DEFENCE PLANNING, DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the statement the hon. member has just made is incorrect and unjustified.

maintopic: DEFENCE POLICY, DEFENCE PLANNING, DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: The hon. member for Trinity has made an interjection that has not been written for him, and it is the first statement he has made that has not made sense. I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that the answer can be found-

maintopic: DEFENCE POLICY, DEFENCE PLANNING, DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: Don't change that in Hansard. You said "that has not made sense."

maintopic: DEFENCE POLICY, DEFENCE PLANNING, DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: May I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the answer can be found not in the research I have done but the research of one who is a very great authority and a leading columnist of that paper to which all members of the opposition subscribe, the Toronto Star, known as the Liberals' bible and the C.C.F.'s friend. May I refer to this article, because apparently a lot of research has been done by Mr. Pierre Berton in connection with his column to be found in the Star on Friday last, February 27. In the first place, I asked myself, what was the inception of A. V. Roe Canada Limited?

maintopic: DEFENCE POLICY, DEFENCE PLANNING, DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. The hon. member is proceeding to read an article written by someone else and published in a newspaper. I believe it is a rule of the house that when an hon. member does that he has to accept the views set out in the article-

maintopic: DEFENCE POLICY, DEFENCE PLANNING, DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: As his own.

maintopic: DEFENCE POLICY, DEFENCE PLANNING, DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: -as his own, and I should like to know whether the hon. member for Rosedale accepts these views as his own and supports them.

maintopic: DEFENCE POLICY, DEFENCE PLANNING, DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for the first time in my life I am delighted to accept views set forth in an article in the Toronto Star. As the hon. member no doubt knows, I have read other views expressed in the Star which have not always had my support. In the first place, what was the inception of A. V. Roe Canada Limited? I quote Sir Roy Dobson from Mr. Berton's article:
"I often used to dream of a little empire in Canada"-Dobson's empire has long since become an established fact-a colossal $300 million holding company, the third largest in the land and one of the big 80 in North American industry.
Then one asks himself, and I am sure members of the house would like to know, when did this enterprise get under way?

maintopic: DEFENCE POLICY, DEFENCE PLANNING, DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: Will you just read the article so we will know what words are from the article and what words are yours?

maintopic: DEFENCE POLICY, DEFENCE PLANNING, DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext:
He can
do what he wants.

maintopic: DEFENCE POLICY, DEFENCE PLANNING, DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: In my short experience in the house this is the first time I have ever received any assistance from the hon. member for Vancouver East, who has just interrupted. Perhaps I can please him by reading many of the relevant parts but in view of the fact that I have the floor I am sure he would not mind if I were to say a word or two sometimes. In the past my hon. friend has been known to express his views and I am sure he would not mind me expressing mine.

maintopic: DEFENCE POLICY, DEFENCE PLANNING, DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: I want to be clear when you are quoting the article and when you are expressing your own views.

maintopic: DEFENCE POLICY, DEFENCE PLANNING, DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext:
Quite right. I quote:
In the light of recent events, I think it's worth while to review this old tale once more. Dobson's dream of a Canadian empire began in 1945 when he came here on behalf of the Hawker-Siddeley group to form a subsidiary company. Hawker-Siddeley has thrived on government contracts, the kind that are procured on a non-competitive basis and wholly subsidized. It's a nice way to do business because there's no risk involved. You're sure of the money and the profit comes off the top.
Then, Mr. Speaker, the next question I asked myself was this: Where did the Hawker-Siddeley group get their capital to operate? How did they begin operations in Canada originally? For my hon. friend, I quote:
Dobson started out in Canada by acquiring an aircraft plant in Malton without putting up a nickel. He borrowed $1,079 from the late Canadian financier, J. P. Bickell, a director of Victory Aircraft. This paid the legal fees. Then, through
[Mr. Walker.)

C. D. Howe, he got Victory Aircraft, into which the Canadian taxpayer had poured more than $7 million. Price to Dobson: $2 million. But he didn't give Howe any money. He simply promised that he'd pay for the plant with 50 per cent of the new company's profits. No profits, no pay.

maintopic: DEFENCE POLICY, DEFENCE PLANNING, DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: I love the quotation. That is the reason I asked.

maintopic: DEFENCE POLICY, DEFENCE PLANNING, DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: This is now myself speaking, for the benefit of the hon. member. Where did they get their capital? I appreciate the good nature of my hon. friend in his interruptions.

maintopic: DEFENCE POLICY, DEFENCE PLANNING, DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: Out of the Canadian taxpayers.

maintopic: DEFENCE POLICY, DEFENCE PLANNING, DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext:
Very well put. My friend anticipates the Star.	Where did they get
their capital to operate? I quote:
He then got $2| million working capital from a bank, through Bickell, and in gratitude made Bickell chairman of the board of the new company. He promised to pay this loan back with the other half of the company's profits. This is nice work if you can get it but I hardly think it comes under the heading of a gamble. It certainly has none of the uncertainty of a poker game or a slot machine or even the uncertainty involved in launching a normal business enterprise in this country.

maintopic: DEFENCE POLICY, DEFENCE PLANNING, DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: Would my hon. friend permit a question?

maintopic: DEFENCE POLICY, DEFENCE PLANNING, DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext:
The end of this quotation is as follows:
Nor would I use the word "courageous" to describe Dobson's bargain basement deal here. ''Bold'', yes. But this hardly makes him the Sir Lancelot of Canadian business.

maintopic: DEFENCE POLICY, DEFENCE PLANNING, DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: Would my hon. friend permit a question?

maintopic: DEFENCE POLICY, DEFENCE PLANNING, DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: That is the end of the quotation.

maintopic: DEFENCE POLICY, DEFENCE PLANNING, DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: He mentioned a man called "Bickell". Has he this gentleman's initials and is he the Mr. Bickell who is closely identified with the Conservative party?

maintopic: DEFENCE POLICY, DEFENCE PLANNING, DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: No.

maintopic: DEFENCE POLICY, DEFENCE PLANNING, DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: He is just as closely identified with the Liberals.

maintopic: DEFENCE POLICY, DEFENCE PLANNING, DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext:
My friend, of course, is just
interjecting his own particular brand of humour. He knows full well because he is a friend of Mr. Ed Bickell who is identified with the Conservative party while the one I am referring to is the late J. P. Bickell.

maintopic: DEFENCE POLICY, DEFENCE PLANNING, DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext:
I just wanted
to make sure.

maintopic: DEFENCE POLICY, DEFENCE PLANNING, DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext:
I am amazed to hear that
because I thought my friend's new testament every morning was the Toronto Star from the night before.
Defence Policy, Planning and Production

maintopic: DEFENCE POLICY, DEFENCE PLANNING, DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: I read the Globe in the morning and the Star at noon.

maintopic: DEFENCE POLICY, DEFENCE PLANNING, DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext:
The next question we ask
as members of the house is this, and this is all very relevant to the debate. What stage of development had the company reached by 1952, for example, or 1954. Again for the benefit of the hon. member for Vancouver East I say "I quote":
One has to admit he had vision, though. And he had faith in Canada. By July, 1952, the people of Canada poured $121 million into A. V, Roe. The Hawker-Siddeley group, which was the sole owner of the company, invested during the same period $10 million. By the end of 1954, more than $480 million in public money had been pumped into A. V. Roe. The total Hawker-Siddeley investment at that point stood at just $16 million.

maintopic: DEFENCE POLICY, DEFENCE PLANNING, DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: Isn't private enterprise wonderful?

maintopic: DEFENCE POLICY, DEFENCE PLANNING, DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext:
I continue:
By this time, Sir Roy's dreams were coming true, his foresight was paying off. The company was spawning other companies and buying into more. It owns eight outright today, has controlling interests in two others, and 250,000 shares in a third, Algoma Steel. It has no funded debt of any kind.
Then, the next question I asked myself as I did this research, from which I was finally saved by this illuminating article was this-I excuse the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) and I do not blame him for leaving the house. Come back in the evening, I will be here at eight o'clock- did anybody else benefit except A. V. Roe Canada Limited? Again I quote from the Toronto Star:
When A. V. Roe became a public company in 1956, some of its directors and executives were allowed to share in the fruits of Sir Roy Dobson's gamble. They were given the option of buying 84,000 shares at $12.50 a share. The following year the stock soared to $25 and so, for those who converted their shares at that time, this was a profitable venture.
Until about a year ago, when the news of sputnik made obvious the fact that the Russians had an intercontinental ballistic missile, Sir Roy Dobson's vision seemed to be working pretty well. From that borrowed thousand he had built an industrial empire which was to receive a total of $1,500 millions from the Canadian taxpayer.
My next question to myself was this: Who sparked the operations in Canada of these various companies? Then, my answer is this, and I quote:
Mr. Crawford Gordon, once C. D. Howe's right-hand man, had been installed as president and general manager. The company had grown to be the biggest member of the parent Hawker-Siddeley group. Many of the subsidiary companies subsisted nicely on government work (Avro Aircraft, Orenda Engines, Canadian Steel Improvements). Others, such as Canadian Car, had government contracts. Dominion Coal and Steel was also subsidized publicly.

maintopic: DEFENCE POLICY, DEFENCE PLANNING, DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext:
And still are.

Defence Policy, Planning and Production

maintopic: DEFENCE POLICY, DEFENCE PLANNING, DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext:
My next question, and I am sure that of the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch), was; did Avro know that the Arrow would be cancelled? I do not know that that is so pertinent today because the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer) said, let us assume that the company must have known last September that the Arrow contract was going to be cancelled. In any event, just to keep the record straight, may I answer from the Toronto Star editorial, and I quote:
But something seems to have gone wrong with Sir Roy's vision at this point for, if we are to believe the statements issued this week, he never at any time had any inkling that a cloud no smaller than an Arrow was in the sky. It was becoming increasingly obvious that the plane was fast becoming obsolete. By fall the government let out the strong hint that the Arrow program was doomed and in a few weeks, newspapermen, military experts, scientists, politicians and the general public were pretty sure it was doomed. In November, indeed, a Toronto financial magazine set to work on an article which assumed that fact. But Sir Roy did not know, he says, because nobody told him.
The next question is: what has Avro done in the last six months to prepare itself for the cancellation of the Arrow contract? We have heard the explanation of the hon. member for Trinity, but he naturally is prejudiced. Whoever it is who writes his speeches is also prejudiced. I want to say this, that I do not profess to be thinking up these answers myself. I admit I am quoting from the Toronto Star. I quote:
The company had six months to do something, after the government's strong hint last fall and it did do something. It started a propaganda campaign to save the Arrow through public opinion and political pressure. The lobby at Ottawa was high level. The campaign, handled by Cockfield-Brown advertising agency, was at all levels. It included a piece by Crawford Gordon himself in Maclean's magazine (the Arrow, said Gordon, was not dead) and a high priced film which was intended to show, subtly, that the Arrow was going strong. Ostensibly the film was supposed to mark the 50th anniversary of flight in Canada but it was mostly about the Arrow. It was offered free to TV stations across the land which might have been expected to run it last Sunday. But Mr. Diefen-baker made his announcement on Friday and that made the film out of date-obsolete.
I inserted the word "obsolete".
There are rumours that Mr. Diefenbalcer had got wind of the film and was furious about it.
Then I asked this question: What did Avro do when the contract was cancelled? I quote:
And Sir Roy-the man of vision? Why, he couldn't have been more surprised! And so he had to fire 13,800 employees all at once, instantly, because, with all that time and all that money and all that vision his company hadn't been able to come up with an alternate plan for putting A. V. Roe into the competitive, non-subsidized aircraft business.

maintopic: DEFENCE POLICY, DEFENCE PLANNING, DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman permit a question?

maintopic: DEFENCE POLICY, DEFENCE PLANNING, DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext:
Yes, indeed, but may I just finish the quotation first?
There were some nasty people who said that Sir Roy and his boys were gambling again and that last week's mass dismissals were an attempt to embarrass the government but Sir Roy has denied that. For as you can see, Sir Roy has never really gambled at all.

maintopic: DEFENCE POLICY, DEFENCE PLANNING, DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: The hon. gentleman said he would now permit my question. What has the government got for the 11,000 men that are out of work because of the action taken by the Prime Minister, regardless of who started Avro or what Avro may have done?

maintopic: DEFENCE POLICY, DEFENCE PLANNING, DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: My friend obviously has not been in the house this past week or he would not have asked that question. We have had that answered fully by the Prime Minister, the Minister of Defence Production (Mr. O'Hurley) and by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Pearkes) himself. They have gone into that subject with such thoroughness that I am amazed the hon. member did not at least read of it in the newspapers.

maintopic: DEFENCE POLICY, DEFENCE PLANNING, DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: The 11,000 are still out of work.

maintopic: DEFENCE POLICY, DEFENCE PLANNING, DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext:
May I call it six o'clock?
At six o'clock the house took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at 8 p.m.

maintopic: DEFENCE POLICY, DEFENCE PLANNING, DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think that we had about finished with the Star, but before sitting down may I quote from the Telegram of Saturday, February 28, page 4. There is an article headed, "The Arrow is the Main Reason I quit-Simonds". Then I quote:
I.t-Gen. Guy Simonds said last night the Avro Arrow was destined to be obsolete before it was started.
Then this is a quote from Lieutenant-General Simonds:
The Liberal government's decision to go ahead with it was a principal reason for my resignation.
Mr. Speaker, so that we can get a clear insight, in answer to my hon. friend from Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) as to what was done with the local people in and around the plant, might I quote from the Brampton Conservator of Thursday, February 26, wherein it sets out a report received from the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Pallett). It is headed, "Pallett's Message to Avro Workers", and it states:
"Jobs for 1,500 people in a new Peel county industry are hinted for the near future," states John Pallet, local member of parliament, in a special delivery letter to the editor of the Conservator. Arriving at press time, the letter follows.

"Dear Bill:
I am enclosing herewith a copy of Hansard of February 23rd, which I believe sets out clearly the basis for the government decision to discontinue the Arrow, and I would refer you to Mr. Pearkes' statement on page 1279 and particularly to the statements on pages 1280, 1281-"

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: DEFENCE POLICY, DEFENCE PLANNING, DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: Order. I trust the hon. member will not read from newspapers something dealing with what has gone on in this house this session, because that would not be in order.

maintopic: DEFENCE POLICY, DEFENCE PLANNING, DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext:
Thank you very much. Suffice it to say that he referred in detail not only to the speech of the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) but also to the speech of the Minister of National Defence. Then he goes on to say:
I personally have been meeting with both union officials and-

maintopic: DEFENCE POLICY, DEFENCE PLANNING, DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: This relates to what a member of the house said outside the house. As I understand it, it was said by a member of the house to the Avro workers.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: DEFENCE POLICY, DEFENCE PLANNING, DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: I think the limitation relates to what is said in the house, not to what is said by members of the house outside the house.

maintopic: DEFENCE POLICY, DEFENCE PLANNING, DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext:
The hon. member for Peel was not recounting to newspapers what happened in the house, and I ask hon. members to note that he spoke to company officials many times over the past few months. He goes on:
At all times in my discussions with them I was quite clear that it was my belief that the program was to be terminated. This decision, affecting as it does so many of my constituents, is one of grave concern to me. However, the steps having been taken, we must deal with the situation as it is.
First of all, most of the employees should be entitled to three weeks' pay at the present time, which would indicate the one week severance pay plus the two weeks' accrued holiday pay.
Secondly, the national employment service have detailed extra people to assist, in the first place to ensure that there will be prompt payments of unemployment insurance claims, and subsequently to assist in finding other jobs. In this they should be successful. The national employment service places about 25 per cent of all the positions filled. Last year in the Toronto metropolitan area-
I ask the hon. members of the house, Mr. Speaker, through you, to note this-
-including Brampton and Oakville, they located 93,000 persons and indicated that in the year 1958 there were in that area a total of 372,000 positions available.
Thirdly, there have been meetings between company officials and government with a view of assessing the capabilities of the plants in the immediate future. Those meetings are going on and it is felt that something may be worked out in this regard.
Mr. Speaker, there is the message of the hon. member for Peel, who for months now,
Defence Policy, Planning and Production since September of last year, has been warning not only the company, which knew it well, but the members of the unions as well. I think we should take that into consideration. May I also get on record, because this is the opportunity, and the last opportunity, to do so, some of the comments of the members in the press gallery. May I first refer to an article by Charles Lynch of the Southam News Service in the Ottawa Citizen of February 25. I quote:
Intentionally or otherwise, they-
Meaning Avro-
-convinced the government that they were trying to go over their heads with a gigantic squeeze play related to the unemployment crisis. Lay-offs in Port Arthur and in Cape Breton by A.V. Roe subsidiaries were made to appear as pressure moves to save the Arrow-a numbers game with jobs as the stakes.
Might I quote too Frank Swanson, the associate editor of the Ottawa Citizen, in an article of February 24:
It seems quite clear, as suspected then, that the decision to abandon the Arrow was actually taken last September. There is reason to feel that Avro was fully aware of the decision, if not then, shortly thereafter.
Might I also refer to an article in the Gazette by that distinguished columnist Arthur Blakely, dated February 26:
From the moment that the government's inclination to discontinue the Arrow first began to be evident, Mr. Gordon mustered all of the resources of his large company to force the government to change its mind. Every means was employed to appeal directly to the public over the government's head. The possible fate of skilled Canadian technicians-the possibility of a substantial addition to unemployment as a result of a single stroke of government policy-these were tossed into the field of public controversy. Canadian pride in an aircraft designed an manufactured in Canada was exploited to the full. As was the spectre of a possible loss of Canadian sovereignty.
These statements, Mr. Speaker, by responsible members of the press gallery would lead one to conclude that the lack of an alternative program to provide employment for the Avro workers and the workers of Orenda, which is the key issue in this whole question, was brought about in large measure by the Avro company devoting their time and the government's money in an attempt to force the government to change its decision rather than using that valuable time and experience, and that great deal of money and effort, in working out some diversification program, some alternative program, or anything at all which would keep those workers employed and still aid the defence production of our country.
As far as the attendant issue of sovereignty is concerned, I think any fair minded person who examined the defence arrangements with

any of the other NATO countries must conclude that this aspect of the argument has been grossly exaggerated. The simple fact remains, as one editorial writer has so well expressed it, that we simply have to "stop spending money which we could not afford for a weapon we did not need".
In conclusion, in citing these editorials might I commend to the house the reading of an editorial by that grand old man of journalism, the proprietor of the Ottawa Journal, Grattan O'Leary, in the issue of February 24, a leading editorial, which really places this matter where it belongs.
Might I say this before the vote is taken that it did not appear to matter to this colossus-because Avro was a colossus-that all parties in this house agreed that the Arrow contract should be terminated. It did not appear to matter to this great colossus that the Arrow had become obsolete before coming into production. It did not appear to matter to them that the Arrow was four years behind in production. It did not appear to matter if hundreds of millions of dollars more had been spent on its production than was anticipated or promised. Nothing mattered to that company which had been spoiled during the years from 1945 onward. It began to feel just as the sacred cow does in India -that the Avro company could do no wrong; that Avro could do what it liked. And it dared the government of Canada to discontinue or sever a contract for a project which had long become obsolete.

speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question?

speechtext:
I should be very glad to, but after I have finished my remarks, because I was interrupted so often before the dinner recess. If the hon. gentleman would allow me to a carry on for three minutes I will be glad to give him an opportunity.
My final word is this. How fortunate we are, how fortunate are hon. members of the party opposite, and hon. members of all parties in this house, that we should have among the heads of our government at this time a minister of defence who is not only brave in battle but, what is equally important, brave in the battle of keeping the peace.

maintopic: DEFENCE POLICY, DEFENCE PLANNING, DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext: You are trying hard for that job as parliamentary secretary.

not only of our great north but of Canada as an integrated part of the NATO program. I appreciate the applause, but I have only 30 seconds left. Our defence policy, despite the criticisms made by some hon. members is to attain security-

maintopic: REQUEST FOR ACTION ON LAY-OFFS AND REDUCED MARKETS
REQUEST FOR ACTION ON LAY-OFFS AND REDUCED MARKETS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the grievance I intend to introduce at this time is based on the failure of the government to take adequate action to meet the demands of the coal industry by introducing adequate measures to take care of the existing crisis causing extensive lay-offs in the industry created by unusual stockpiles and declining markets. The coal situation today offers a major problem, a problem so serious that it can be described as a crisis.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: REQUEST FOR ACTION ON LAY-OFFS AND REDUCED MARKETS
speechtext: Would the hon. member give the house a minute to settle down so that we can hear.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR ACTION ON LAY-OFFS AND REDUCED MARKETS
speechtext:
I was just saying that the coal situation today offers a major problem, a problem so serious that it can be described as a crisis, a crisis which has been most prominent over the last 18 months. Before dealing with the specific point of lay-offs and declining markets, I should like first to introduce my remarks by bringing to the attention of the house remarks made by the former prime minister, Right Hon. Louis St.


Laurent, remarks which have been quoted in the house and have been strongly criticized by members on the government side, particularly during the last two election campaigns. Addressing a political meeting in Fredericton, the then prime minister said:
Now, will maritime coal continue to be the cheapest fuel for the production of power for all time? I do not think it will. I think that coal is going to become more valuable for chemical and synthetical processes than it will be as a fuel. In the meantime, of course, we want these coal mines kept in operation because we do not want the coal mining towns to become ghost towns. But so far as I am concerned, so far as my opinions may carry weight in the decisions that are taken, we are not going to encourage substantial increase in the production of coal because I do not think that that would be fair to future generations of Canadians.
And the then prime minister could have added-"to the present generation". There, Mr. Speaker, was a prime minister who, notwithstanding the critical significance of and possible reaction to his remarks, would rather tell the truth than adopt the position of his opponents by making promises which he knew then he would never be able to fulfil.
The members on the government side of this house, and especially those from Nova Scotia, are familiar with the election ads of their party which appeared in the Halifax Mail Star of June 8, 1957, which were entitled, "Action Today or Regret Tomorrow". Last June, when the temporary lay-offs in the Nova Scotia coal mines were not avoided by definite action by this government, we of the official opposition introduced a motion of non-confidence expressing our regret that the government had failed to avert a five-week lay-off in the Nova Scotia coal mines, and that the government had walked away from its promises to promote the development of industry in the Atlantic provinces. In the course of that debate, which took place only eight months ago, we were told by the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan) that we in the opposition were not serious when we said that the surplus stockpile of 1,400,000 tons might not be sold during the coming year.
The minister clearly stated that the truth of the matter was that the company was selling more coal than was sold before. The minister further stated, and he repeated, that the truth of the matter was that there were orders for over 4,600,000 tons of coal. He further claimed that with the leadership and aggressive management of the company, and the co-operation of the government, 350,000 tons of coal had been sold to new customers and that new markets had been developed in the province of Ontario. He strongly affirmed that with orders on hand for 4,600,000 tons

of coal, and orders still coming in, the whole stockpile would be liquidated.
Farther along in the course of his remarks he said that one of the reasons that the layoff was not averted was because the government was not consulted about a lay-off of five weeks. I want the minister's exact words to go on the record. They appear on page 1801 of Hansard for July 1, 1958. These are the words of the Minister of National Revenue:
What was the situation? We were told that we did not avert a lay-off of five weeks. We did not have an opportunity to avert a lay-off of five weeks. We were not consulted about a lay-off of five weeks. The company told us that a lay-off of five weeks was necessary for the efficient and economical management of the company's properties.
What is taking place today in the coal industry? Do we find action today on the promises of the Conservative candidates in the last election or will there be regrets tomorrow? Where are those promises of the Conservative party candidates made on June 8, 1957? In New Brunswick, for example, the statistics will show that in 1957 the total production of coal was 976,597 tons; in 1958, the production is down to 768,465, or a decrease of 207,692 tons. What is coal production in Nova Scotia? In 1957 the statistics will show that the total production was 5,685,770 tons, and in 1958 it is down to 5,254,736, a decrease of 431,034 tons. What will be the results for the year 1959? Well, Mr. Speaker, after the Conservative "Lent" started 10 days before the actual opening of Lent 4,100 coal miners were laid off, so we can expect that production in 1959 will again be much lower than it was in 1958. Where is this definite action being taken by the government as promised to increase the production of coal or even to avert a decrease in production and lay-offs?
I know that a week or so ago the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond (Mr. Mac-Lellan), for example, gave a rosy picture of the situation to this house in so far as his constituency was concerned. He reminded us then that in the maritimes the people were saying, "Beware of Grits bearing gifts." But, Mr. Speaker, I am just back from the maritimes and I can inform this house that what we are hearing in the maritimes today is, "Beware of the Tories and their promises."
I should like to expose to this house the present attitude of the government toward a crisis which is their responsibility. On page 522 of Hansard for January 30, 1959, I asked the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys (Mr. Comtois) the following question:
In view of the statement made by the minister that he has asked for definite recommendations from the chairman of the dominion coal board, will the minister make inquires to determine
Requested Action in Coal Industry whether A. V. Roe made specific proposals to the dominion coal board respecting methods to prevent such a lay-off, and if such proposals were made will the minister tell us on what date and also if the proposals have been dealt with by the coal board?
It is very important that the reply of the minister be inserted at this point. I received from the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys the following reply:
In reply to the last part of the question asked by the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Robi-chaud), I should say that around November 19, 1958 the dominion coal board received representations from Dosco and from the miners union. That meeting dealt solely with the coal marketing situation in Nova Scotia. It is only later that the dominion coal board met several times, between December 8 and December 11, with the parties concerned, to go into this matter. There was no question at the time of cuts in either the payroll or the production. It is only on December 19 that we had a meeting, as I have already said, with Dosco representatives and Premier Stanfield. At that time, the matter of increased assistance to coal producers was discussed and we were told, as we had been in any case in a letter dated December 17-which was produced on the 19th at that meeting-that even if the government decided to boost subsidies, there would probably be a cut in personnel for 40 days, that is to say there would be 40 days' unemployment in the next few months. No decision has yet been taken about the proposals submitted in connection with coal production or its shipping, and even if a decision had been taken, it would concern only the opening of the forthcoming season of navigation.
Mr. Speaker, I have here an article which appeared in the Financial Post under date December 13, 1958, a month and a half before the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys gave me his reply in the house. This article in the Financial Post is entitled, "No Markets, Close Mines: View if Subsidies Denied". I want to read two or three paragraphs of the said article.
Canada's east coast coal industry is on the verge of important decisions-government and private. Increased subventions on maritime coal to permit deeper penetration into vast central Canadian industrial markets are being sought this week in Ottawa.
With huge stockpiles posing problems in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, delegates representing producers, mine unions and provincial governments are pressing their case before the dominion coal board.
They are requesting subsidy increases ranging as
high as $2 a ton. Maximum subvention is now $5.25 a ton.
If increases are not granted, there could be some drastic revisions in mining and marketing policy by big operators.
Mr. Speaker, we have a right to know what was the nature of the request placed before the dominion coal board by the Dominion Steel and Coal Corporation. Is the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan) or the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys in a position to state that at this time they were not consulted before the lay-off took place, as

Requested Action in Coal Industry the Minister of National Revenue indicated in this house on July 1 of last year? What is the present government doing about the present crisis? What has it done to avert the present lay-off, or to avert further lay-offs? Further meetings have taken place. Requests have been presented before the dominion coal board and before the government by the miners union, by municipal councils, by the provincial government of Nova Scotia, by the minister of mines for Nova Scotia, and by the premier of Nova Scotia, and even at this late date we are still unable to get any word from the government, from the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) or from the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys as to their decision following these requests. As far back as November 19 last the dominion coal board had been receiving representations from Dosco and from the miners' union and also from the other sources which I have stated.
Between December 8 and December 11 further representations were again made on this subject. On December 19 another meeting took place, this time with Dosco representatives, and they were accompanied by Premier Stanfield of Nova Scotia. On February 2 a third meeting was held, when a Nova Scotian delegation headed for the second time by Premier Stanfield conferred with the Prime Minister and other federal ministers. What were the results of this meeting? We learned in the Montreal Gazette of February 3 that a statement was made by Premier Stanfield, but not by the Prime Minister or the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys. In this statement the premier of Nova Scotia stated, as reported in the Montreal Gazette for February 3:
Maritime coal industry may seek federal assistance.
I want just to quote a few paragraphs of this article:
The premier told reporters later he urged increased subventions on an emergency basis as the best means of staving off further lay-offs.
He had supported, he said, proposals made by Dosco earlier to the dominion coal board.
While the premier would make no guess as to how much additional federal money this might involve, informants said it would be around $4,000,000 a year.
Over a month has gone by since this delegation met in Ottawa, and still we are unable to get any decision or reply from the government. Mr. Speaker, this is nothing else but another example of the confusion, indecision, and this time not only of delayed action but of relayed action by the present government.
It is true that on February 6 the hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) addressed a question to the Prime Minister,

and on this occasion he received the following reply, which is reported on page 754 of Hansard of that date:
Mr. Speaker, a few days ago a delegation from Nova Scotia consisting of the premier of that province and other representatives, met with me and other ministers in connection with the situation resulting from the glut in coal and the stockpiling of some 1,200,000 tons or more.
A general discussion took place. The views of the people present were listened to, and consideration is being given to whatever action may be taken to the end that the situation may be met. In saying this I am not indicating at the moment what if any action will be taken. Certainly the representations were of such a nature and were so reasonably and fully made that they deserve the fullest consideration, and this they are receiving.
Again I repeat that so far the poor miners in the coal industry have to be satisfied with nothing else but consideration, and consideration in due course.
We of the opposition are being accused of criticizing the government and of offering no suggestion, or no constructive suggestion, which could take care of a situation such as the one we are discussing tonight. Since the opening of this session we have had thrown at us time after time by members on the government side the very same question: What would you do? A similar situation existed in West Germany a few months ago, and what action was taken by the West German government? In the first place, a government embargo was placed on the issuance of new coal import licences. Second, tax exemptions were granted to the coal mining industry, trying to make coal competitive with fuel oil. Third, the government of West Germany promised grants for 500 million marks, which represents $120 million, to increase coal consumption.
A similar situation existed in the United Kingdom, and there again definite action and planning took place. A report originating from London, as produced in the Halifax Chronicle Herald for Saturday, February 28, reads as follows:
Britain's coal miners Friday adopted a four-point policy aimed at fighting a current slump in the industry and a drift away from coal to other fuels. Union leaders representing the 700,000 workers in the nationalized industry agreed on the program at a three-hour session Friday. The main points are:
1.	The government should re-examine present plans for developing nuclear energy as a power source.
2.	Oil policy should be revised, reducing imports and switching electricity power stations from oil back to coal. Fuel oil taxes should be increased.
3.	The system of distributing coal to consumers, left in the hands of private enterprise when the state took over the coal mines in 1947, also should be nationalized.
4.	More research should be carried out on finding additional uses for coal.

I am not proposing to the government that all these suggestions made in the United Kingdom should be adopted, but the fact remains that the Canadian government is today facing a crisis which requires straightforward action. It affects 10,000 coal miners. It affects a basic industry in an area which has a population of over 100,000 people. It affects the entire area of a province where practically no other industry exists. It is true that the situation in New Brunswick may not be as bad as it is at the present time, in Nova Scotia, but nevertheless in the last three or four months of 1958 the coal miners in the Minto area were able to work for only two or three days a week. Fortunately, in the mid-winter months, the entire supply of coal could be taken by the New Brunswick power commission. However, in view of the statements being made in the province about the possibility that the thermal plants to be built in future will use oil instead of coal, notwithstanding the statements which have been made in this house the future of the New Brunswick coal industry is not bright.
It is true that Canada is importing close to 20 million tons of coal annually from the United States and that if less than 10 per cent of this demand could be diverted to Nova Scotia the problem would be practically solved. Where is that market in Ontario for maritime coal which was promised last June? I should like to ask the members of the government whether we can have an assurance that the market which was promised in Ontario last year still exists. I feel that the action taken by the government with regard to the coal industry is too limited. I have here a press clipping from the Financial Times dated July 11, 1958. It bears the heading "Coal Mining should be in Borden^ Commission Field". According to this report it seems that the government has not taken the interest in coal that the question deserves. The last paragraph of this article reads as follows:
It would indeed be a pity if coal mining were now removed from the context of the studies which Canadians had every right to expect would cover all forms of energy. Coal mining needs such a study; probably more than any of the other branches of the energy industries group.
What has been done by the government to bring new industries to the maritimes? What has been done by the company and by the government to increase sales of coal? It is true it is a surplus of industrial coal which is creating the main difficulty at the moment, but it is difficult to understand why, when there is such a surplus, there should be in the maritimes today an evident shortage of domestic coal. I have in my hand two letters which have been written by a Mr. J. W.
66968-9-100
Requested Action in Coal Industry Patterson of Charlottetown. The first letter is dated February 3, 1959, and reads in part as follows:
Orders accepted in September, 1958, were received only late in December.
The second letter dated February 5, 1959 is also signed by the same Mr. Patterson and reads in part as follows:
There is a shortage of Nova Scotia coal here. Small dealers will be forced out of business if something is not done.
This situation exists in my own constituency of Gloucester. We read of two or three different occasions in the month of January on which the city of Moncton had to import United States coal because it could not get a supply from the Nova Scotia coal mines. It seems that the company is not making the effort which it should to dispose of its surplus coal production. We all recognize that coal is one of our great natural resources. Coal mining, as Premier Stanfield reminded officials of the A. V. Roe company last year, is more than an industry in Nova Scotia. As he said, it is the staff of life for many communities in the province, something much more than just a matter of dollars and cents.
As a representative of a constituency in the Atlantic provinces I have a strong feeling that no distinction should be made between the ways of protecting certain particular industries-however important these industries may be to the economy of central Canada-and the coal industry which is vital to the economy of Nova Scotia and to one section of New Brunswick.
If effective government action is required for an area of Canada which enjoys a diversified industrial economy, why should the same principle not apply to a less favoured area which depends almost entirely upon one industry? The government may be acting wisely in granting subsidies or even additional subsidies in order to favour the transportation of coal to Ontario in competition with substantial imports of United States coal. The people of the maritime provinces and the coal miners of my area are just as concerned with the lay-offs which have taken place in their industry, and the further layoffs which are contemplated, as the A. V. Roe workers are concerned about the lay-offs to which they were subjected last week in the Toronto area.
It is my feeling-and here again I am in complete agreement with the statement made by the former prime minister, the Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent-that it is the duty of the government to see to it that the coal miners of Nova Scotia are kept at work and that the mining towns of Nova Scotia do not become ghost towns. I feel that action should be
1574	HOUSE OF COMMONS
Requested Action in Coal Industry taken in the present situation, even if it means substantial tax concessions or other forms of assistance in this particular area of Nova Scotia, to provide a new industry with coal as its basis which would at least restore the economy of the industry to its 1957 level and alleviate this atmosphere of uncertainty, this fear and gloom which prevail in Cape Breton today.
If, for example, 1,000 or even 2,000 coal miners could be retired from the mines and provided with work at industrial plants located at the pit heads the problem would be solved for years to come. I therefore strongly urge the government to give this matter very serious consideration. It is true that fewer miners would mean less production, but it would also mean that the problem of the surplus would not be so great and that the stockpile would not be so formidable. The policy now being followed by the government makes it evident that the present stockpiles cannot be disposed of. If a coal surplus is to be a continuing problem, then we ask the government, in the name of the miners concerned, to tell us the truth. Let the government come out and give us the facts. If they made a mistake with regard to the promises they made during the last two elections, let the government come out today and explain the situation as it now exists.
The Avro company should have been influenced to establish in Cape Breton and not near Montreal their proposed steel rolling plant. The government should have intervened and provided the company with every argument and if need be even financial assistance in order to influence it to open this new mill in the Atlantic provinces in the vicinity of the coal mining area.
I have here the famous document known as the seven Atlantic resolutions. If some of these statements were put into practice today the problem would be practically solved. Let the government in the face of the present crisis take the action it promised. Let it take this action today because if it does not do so it will regret it tomorrow. We are asking the government to put into force at this very moment the second of the Atlantic resolutions, either by placing a more equitable share of defence contract expenditures within the Atlantic provinces or, if no such contract exists today as we can see by the policy of the present government, it should consider the establishment there of crown corporations. Another way of implementing the second Atlantic resolution would be-and this particular sentence of that resolution applies directly to the present situation:
[Mr. Roblchaud.l
-by encouraging local enterprises to locate in the area and to encourage the processing in the area of our natural resources as a result of special fiscal considerations.
Another means of implementing these resolutions would be through the government giving serious consideration to the request of the unions to establish a marketing board to take care of the disposal of surplus coal production.
If we look at what is happening to our coal mines in Nova Scotia and our base metal mines in New Brunswick we have good reason to ask the present government to divert a part of its northern vision to the maritime provinces. The government has an opportunity to act now. If it does not act today it will regret not doing so tomorrow. There may be a limit to government subventions but the seriousness of the situation must be an important factor in influencing the decision of the government. This government as well as the previous administration has not hesitated when it came to the question of grants and subsidies for the grain producers of the prairie provinces. It did not hesitate to offer assistance to some displaced technical employees at the Avro plant. The government should not hesitate to take action with respect to the coal industry.
Further research into the use of coal is now a matter of urgent importance and a full investigation in the field of research should be undertaken at once. A delegation of Canadian scientists should be sent to Europe and particularly to West Germany and the United Kingdom to study the possibilities of chemical uses of coal.
Special concessions or even subventions should be granted to the establishment of industries in the Cape Breton area, industries which will use coal as the basis of operation and operate in conjunction with the existing steel mill already established in that area. It is evident that the people of the maritimes are not satisfied with the attitude of Avro but at least in the last few days the president of Dosco, a subsidiary of Avro, gave to the miners and the people concerned a true picture of the situation as he sees it. The coal miners are paying their share in supporting industries in central Canada and it is the duty of the central government to protect the economy of an area with a per capita income substantially below the national average.
In closing I wish to repeat that the Gordon commission concluded that the main market for coal should remain in the maritimes, and there it should remain for the good of the maritimes and for the good of Canada. It is the responsibility of the government to take definite and effective action to solve

the present coal problem and again I remind the government that we want action now. We want a decision to be announced tomorrow not later than the period before orders of the day are called because if action is not taken at this time the government will soon regret it's failure to act as it has promised to do in this particular case.

Mr. Speaker, in his remarks the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Robichaud) referred to a speech I made in the house a few weeks ago dealing with the economic situation in Nova Scotia. My remarks at that time did not relate to the coal industry, which is in a bad situation as everyone admits. They related to the extra help which has been given to the maritime provinces by the government in terms of grants to the provinces and specifically to the important added support and help we received under federal-provincial cost sharing programs.
As far as the coal situation is concerned, we are very worried about it I assure you, Mr. Speaker, much more so than the hon. member for Gloucester who, as the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Mac-Innis) has just said, seems to me to be more interested in making a political game out of this question than anything else.
Before going any further, I should say that the problem we have now in the coal industry in Nova Scotia and in Cape Breton island is not news. It is not something that has developed overnight. It developed during the last 10 years when the Liberal party was in power, when something should have been done and when nothing was done to assist our coal industry. The problem we are facing today could have been averted by planned action five or six years ago; it could have been averted after the war by some assistance to regain the 900,000 ton market for coal in Ontario which we lost during the war and while that government was in power. When the Liberals were in power they gave some assistance to the coal industry in Nova Scotia; but it consisted only of loans to help mechanize the mines. I would think that anyone with a particle of a brain would know that lending to assist mechanization to increase production in itself could never be enough. In the very fact that they did not help us to find a larger market for this increased production and to give us a stable market in normal times lies the great tragedy of our coal situation in Nova Scotia; and therein is the great default of the Liberal party to Nova Scotia.
Since this government came into power it has given substantial, tangible help to our
Requested Action in Coal Industry Nova Scotian coal industry. I am not going to list all these new aids tonight. Briefly, since the Conservative administration came into power we have had subventions that helped us to sell 500,000 tons of coal in Ontario last year and to regain some of the market that was lost during the time that the previous administration was in office. We have acquired substantial preference for Nova Scotia coal in government buildings across this country. We saw coal subventions approved, even finally agreed to by the Liberals at the last moment before an election, to move coal to thermal-power plants in the maritime provinces. This was the first real help in these provinces in 10 years to our vital Nova Scotian industry. The tragedy is that the change in government took place after it was too late to avert the terrible problem we now have in Cape Breton and other parts of Nova Scotia.
Just what is the situation with regard to the coal industry? It is not a Nova Scotian situation; it is an all-Canadian situation, a national situation. Since 1948 there has been a decrease of 17J million tons in the consumption of coal in Canada. In 1948 there was a market in Canada for 47J million tons of coal. By 1958 that market had gone down to 30 million tons. What is the reason for that? First of all, the railways were dieselized which meant the loss of a market for 7J million tons of coal. This of course, was done during the Liberal administration without any attempt at all to find a new market for the coal that was replaced. At the same time advancements in natural gas and in the development of oil distribution have meant that we have a domestic market for 10 million tons less coal now than in 1948.
This is a fact that has to be faced. Over the last 18 months the government moved to help this situation in every way it could. Actually the extra subventions granted last year and the other help made available to the Nova Scotia coal industry in a normal year could have averted the lay-offs we have now in Cape Breton. The new subventions would have been sufficient in a normal year.
But last year the coal industry was faced with a special situation. For one thing a market we had for approximately 300,000 tons of coal in pulp mills and hydro plants in the province of Quebec was lost to us in 1958 because of high water and the availability of electricity as a source of power. In addition, there was increased production of coal in 1958 in the Cape Breton mines. Along with these things there has been a certain industrial decline in the nation which meant that there was not quite the market for coal last year that there was the year before.

Requested Action in Coal Industry
What this means in actual figures is that there is now a stockpile of 1,200,000 tons of coal for which there is no purchaser available. This has happened despite the subvention help provided last year. But I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that without that aid the problem in the Cape Breton mines today would be very much greater than it is.
Every Nova Scotia member, as all hon. members well know, has been pressing the government to give us the additional aid which we need, particularly over the next few years, to help us to maintain our coal industry. We feel that we do not need this aid indefinitely. We believe that it will only be a stopgap until the natural expansion of the country will reinstate a market for our coal. For example, we will be using a greater amount of coal between 1970 and 1980 simply because oil and gas will have become more expensive, and coal will be in a better position to compete. It is expected that our coal will not only have a substantial market but will be necessary for turning the wheels of industry within the next 20 years and, as a matter of fact, if we do not have that coal we will be very badly off within a very few years.
The present situation, as Mr. A. L. Fairley president of Dosco said in Glace Bay the other day, is that the short term outlook for our coal industry is not good. Even if the increase which the company is seeking were provided it could not avert the present layoff which was required to offset the surplus stockpile of coal as a result of the unusual economic circumstances last year. But in the future Canada will need the coal of Nova Scotia. In the future the only source of coal available to Ontario and Quebec particularly for the production of hydro power will be found in Nova Scotia. The only other deposits of coal in Canada are in Alberta much too far from the central industrial provinces to provide a source of energy and fuel.
I say then that we base our argument for subventions, not only on the fact that Nova Scotia miners need help and work must be provided in the mines today but also on the fact that in the years to come Canada is going to need the large resources of coal that are available in Nova Scotia. As far as Nova Scotia is concerned, coal mining is our first industry. It accounts for 75 per cent to 80 per cent of our mineral wealth and is worth about $68 million a year to the people of the province. There is no other single mechanical industry employing as many people. We must have assistance now to keep the industry going and to keep our miners there. Some Canadians may think that if Nova Scotia coal cannot now find a market in Canada, although

it will in later years, the mines should be shut down as was suggested by the former prime minister in order to save the coal until 1980 when it will be needed. The last prime minister in a speech in New Brunswick recognized that there would be a big demand for our coal in the years to come. His suggestion was that the coal should be preserved for future generations.
The fallacy of that argument and the reason that subventions are needed now to protect our coal industry is that our mines in Nova Scotia are submarine mines. Unless the pumps continue to operate and unless the mines are maintained there will be no mines in the years to come. Furthermore, the miners of Cape Breton are highly technical personnel. They are men who know how to extract coal and extract it efficiently, so efficiently that over a period of 10 years they have raised their production per man day from 1.6 tons to 2.6 tons, a phenomenal achievement but still not enough to produce coal at a price that will make it competitive with oil and gas. We must keep our miners available to the industry.
We need subventions. We need help to preserve our industry not only for the present but for the future. It is on this basis that we have all joined to impress upon the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) and the cabinet the urgent need for subventions for our coal. I should like to thank the Prime Minister and the cabinet most heartily for the consideration they have given to this urgent problem at a time when they are faced with many other demands from other parts of the nation.

speakeroldname: Hon. George C. Nowlan (Minister of National Revenue):
maintopic: REQUEST FOR ACTION ON LAY-OFFS AND REDUCED MARKETS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have had an interesting contribution to the discussion of this problem tonight and certainly in the six or seven minutes left to me under the rules of the house I cannot develop the over-all problem in any way whatsoever. I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Maclnnis) and the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond (Mr. MacLellan) upon the contribution which they have made to this problem. After all, this is essentially a Nova Scotia problem and all the Nova Scotia members are vitally interested in it and are working in every way possible to achieve a solution. As was pointed out by both hon. members, this problem is not new. It is not something which arose the day before yesterday, nor is it something which arose under this government. I can remember in my early days in Halifax when I was the youngest member of the legislature there were strikes in the mines in Cape Breton and labour difficulties which arose there and the mounted police had to be brought in to deal with them.
We have had a long series of problems in connection with Nova Scotia coal, as is true, of course, of coal mines all over the world. The hon. member for Inverness-Richmond put on the record certain figures concerning the diminution in the consumption of coal. I think hon. members of this house should
Requested Action in Coal Industry look at them and consider just what has happened to this great industry in the last few years. He pointed out that there has been a reduction of over 17 million tons in the use of coal. Why has this occurred? There are three essential reasons. The first one is the dieselization of Canadian National Railways, followed by the Canadian Pacific, so that you have Canadian National locomotives going into Cape Breton coal mines burning oil and hauling coal out to Ontario. This was one of the policies established by the preceding government. I am not saying that these decisions were wrong, I am simply pointing out the economic developments that have taken place. This decision, as the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond pointed out, has cost the Nova Scotia coal mines more that a million tons per year.
Another factor is the gas pipe line about which we heard something in the not too distant past in this chamber. It may be economically justified, and I am not debating that for the moment. However, when you have surplus quantities of gas being brought down to the end of the pipe line, as is now the case, with no established market for it and having it dumped on the market at any price it may bring, that in itself results in a tremendous loss in the consumption of coal.
The third matter is connected with the burning of oil instead of coal. In that connection it is rather significant, and I point this out, that when the dominion coal board was organized after the Carroll commission not too many years ago, 76.5 per cent of all energy used in Canada was derived from coal. In 1957 only 25 per cent of that energy was derived from coal. Petroleum, which accounted for very little of the energy supplied at the time the coal board was formed, was supplying 56.4 per cent of all the energy consumed in Canada in 1957. These are some of the factors which have entered into this situation with which we are confronted tonight, and with which the coal miners of Nova Scotia are confronted.
I should like to point this out, Mr. Speaker, that in 1958, despite this acceleration in competition, despite oil, despite the dieselization, despite gas, despite the high water level to which the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond referred and which resulted in the loss of the equivalent of 250,000 tons of coal and the substitution therefor of electrical energy fed into industrial furnaces; despite all that, last year Nova Scotia had the highest record of employment for miners of any other coal field in North America or in Europe. The reason for that is the subvention policy of this government which provided increased

Requested Action in Coal Industry markets for that coal. There is no question about that, and I have the comparative figures here.
I am not going to take the time of the house to put all these figures on the record. Last year the average days worked by miners in all mines in the United States was 203. It had been much higher and had fallen consistently until last year. In Pennsylvania, it was 208 days and in West Virginia, 219 days. However, in Nova Scotia, removed, as it is from the economic centre of this country and facing these various competitions to which I have referred, the average employment of the miners was 238 days per year. As I say, this was higher than anywhere else in North America and higher than any place in Europe.
This problem that we are facing, of course, is common all over the western world. There are riots in Great Britain, troubles in Germany and in the United States because of unemployment in coal fields. It is a problem that requires a tremendous amount of study, the exercise of judgment and courage in trying to achieve a solution. I agree entirely with the hon. members who have spoken here before that given a period of a few years there is an expanding and continuing market for coal in Canada, and particularly for that produced in Nova Scotia. But at the moment, all I can say is that this present Canadian government is expending more money on subventions than has ever been spent by any government heretofore. We have done more to maintain employment and develop the production of coal in Nova Scotia than any government has done in the past.
This policy, Mr. Speaker, will be continued. As has been suggested here, there are studies going on at the moment. What the ultimate solution will be is not for me to say. I cannot say; it is a matter of study and determination. The people of Nova Scotia, hon. members in this house and the people generally, can rest assured that every possible attention is being paid to this problem and a solution will be worked out. It may not be an entirely satisfactory one because there is no solution which can be entirely satisfactory. However, a solution will be worked out whereby the industry will be protected, will
be maintained in the best way possible in the economic circumstances with which we are faced at the moment.

subtopic: NOTE FROM CANADIAN CHARGE D'AFFAIRES, WASHINGTON, TO ACTING SECRETARY OF STATE

speechtext: Canadian Embassy

The Canadian charge d'affaires a.i. presents his compliments to the acting secretary of state and has the honour to refer to the Canadian embassy's Note No. 624 of October 20, 1958, which set out the views of the Canadian government and the importance it attaches to unrestricted access for Canadian oil to United States markets.
It is understood that the government of the United States is giving consideration to replacing the present voluntary oil import program, which has been extended to February 28, 1959, with a system of mandatory restrictions. The Canadian charge d'affaires wishes to draw to the attention of the acting secretary of state that the views of the Canadian government, as set out in the note referred to above, and as put before representatives of the United States in the meetings of the joint United States-Canadian committee on trade and economic affairs in Ottawa on January 5 and 6, have not changed.
The Canadian government continues to believe that there is no justification on grounds of security (or, for that matter, on the other grounds) for United States restrictions on oil imports from Canada. United States government restrictions on oil imports from Canada, imposed in peacetime for security reasons, are not reconcilable with the need of Canada and the United States to pool their oil resources in time of common emergency. Any system of import restrictions applied against Canadian oil must have an adverse effect on Canadian-United States relations; a system of mandatory controls on imports from Canada, related to security considerations, would be even more disturbing to Canada than would a system of voluntary controls of similar effect.
The Canadian charge d'affaires would request that the views of the Canadian government set forth above be brought to the attention of those concerned with the current review of the United States oil import program.
A. E. Ritchie.
Washington, D.C.
February 19, 1959.
Wednesday, March 4, 1959
